A cultivated man who knew several languages, he had long opposed the company's revenue policies — and when the 1857 uprising broke out, the eighty-year-old Raja answered the call of the nation.

He raised the flag of revolt in Arrah and, with a small force of his men, held the town against a British column that had come to crush him. In the fight at Arrah his left arm was shattered by a bullet — and in a famous act of iron will, he cut off the arm with his own sword so that he could continue the fight.

After his victory, Kunwar Singh crossed into central India, joining the wider revolt before returning to Jagdishpur, where he defeated the British once more. Worn out by his wounds and his year of war, he died in April 1858 — but his last battle, won with a wounded body and a broken arm, made him the eternal symbol of the age's defiance.

coreIdeas.text: He rose against the British at the age of eighty.

coreIdeas.title: The Battle of Arrah
coreIdeas.text: His men held the town against a British column.

coreIdeas.title: The Severed Arm

coreIdeas.title: The Final Victory
coreIdeas.text: He defeated the British at Jagdishpur days before his death.

coreIdeas.title: The First War of Independence
coreIdeas.text: A chief of the great 1857 uprising.

items.legacy: Kunwar Singh is honoured across Bihar as the lion of 1857 — the octogenarian who proved that the love of freedom knows no age. His statue stands at Jagdishpur, his name is given to roads and honours across the state, and his story remains one of the most stirring tales of the first war of independence.

items.name: Jatindranath Mukherjee
items.tagline: Bagha Jatin — the tiger who dared to plan armed revolution
items.attribution: Jatindranath Mukherjee — 'Bagha Jatin'
items.quote: We shall not die for the empire — we shall live for the freedom of Bhārat.
items.summary: Bagha Jatin — 'the tiger' — was the greatest revolutionary leader of Bengal, a man of colossal strength and iron discipline who planned nothing less than an armed rising against the British. He earned his name by killing a tiger with his bare hands, and gave his life in the famous gun-battle at Balasore in 1915, where he fought the entire might of the empire and fell like a soldier.
overview: Born in Kushtia in 1879, Jatindranath Mukherjee grew into a man of legendary strength — a wrestler and athlete whose physical power became the talk of Bengal. His nickname 'Bagha Jatin' came from a hunting incident: when a tiger attacked his party, he killed the beast with his bare hands and a knife, saving his companions.

He joined the revolutionary movement against the British and rose to lead it, believing that freedom would come not by petition but by arms. During the First World War he organised a plan for a rising with German help — arms, men, and a strike against the empire from within — a conspiracy so dangerous that the British made his capture their highest priority.

Betrayed, Jatin and his companions were cornered in a mango grove at Balasore in September 1915. In the gun-battle that followed, he fought the British forces for nearly an hour — wounded again and again but refusing to surrender — until he fell, fatally wounded, asking only that his body be given a decent burial. The British themselves saluted the courage of the man they had hunted for years.

coreIdeas.text: The tiger — he killed a tiger with his bare hands.

coreIdeas.title: Armed Revolution
coreIdeas.text: He planned an armed rising against the empire.

coreIdeas.title: The War Conspiracy
coreIdeas.text: The 1915 plan to strike at the British in wartime.

coreIdeas.title: The Battle of Balasore

coreIdeas.title: The Soldier's Death
coreIdeas.text: He fell fighting, saluted even by his enemies.

items.legacy: Bagha Jatin is the lion of the armed struggle of Bengal — the revolutionary who proved that the spirit of Bhārat could not be crushed by any force. His name is honoured in every account of the freedom movement, his battle at Balasore is remembered as one of the bravest last stands of the era, and his courage remains the standard of the revolutionary ideal.

items.name: Pulina Behari Das
items.tagline: The founder of the first revolutionary group of Bengal
items.attribution: Pulina Behari Das — the founder of Anushilan Samiti
items.quote: Organise the youth, train the body, and fill the mind with the love of the motherland.
items.summary: Pulina Behari Das was the organiser who built the first revolutionary society of Bengal — the Anushilan Samiti — which trained thousands of young men in the physical culture and revolutionary spirit that would shake the empire. His gymnasiums and secret societies prepared the generation that carried the armed struggle of Bengal for two decades.
overview: Born in Faridpur in 1877, Pulina Behari Das grew up in the years when the idea of swaraj, self-rule, was taking fire in Bengal. A man of physical strength and fierce patriotism, he founded the Anushilan Samiti — an organisation of young men trained in lathi-play, wrestling, and drill, whose real purpose was the preparation of revolutionaries.

The Samiti spread across Bengal, opening branches and gymnasiums where hundreds of young men were schooled in courage, discipline, and the love of the motherland. From its ranks came the revolutionaries who attacked British officials, planned risings, and kept the flame of armed resistance burning through the first decades of the twentieth century.

Betrayed by informers, Pulina Behari was arrested in 1910 in the famous trial that followed the bombing of the Viceroy's procession, and sentenced to transportation. He spent years in the Andamans and in jails, and after his release remained a patriot to the end, dying in 1949 — having given Bengal its first organised revolutionary movement.

coreIdeas.text: The first great revolutionary organisation of Bengal.

coreIdeas.title: Physical Culture
coreIdeas.text: Gymnasiums and training that built a generation of fighters.

coreIdeas.title: The Secret Society
coreIdeas.text: Discipline and secrecy in the service of the motherland.

coreIdeas.title: The Teacher of Revolution
coreIdeas.text: His trainees led the armed struggle for decades.

items.legacy: Pulina Behari Das is remembered as the founder of Bengal's organised revolutionary movement — the man whose gymnasiums and societies trained the youth who carried the armed struggle forward. His Anushilan Samiti became the model for revolutionary organisation across Bhārat, and his name remains honoured in the history of the freedom movement.

items.name: Garuda Sadashiva Rao
items.tagline: The freedom fighter of Karnataka who gave his all for the nation
items.attribution: Garuda Sadashiva Rao
items.quote: The nation first — before comfort, before family, before everything.
items.summary: Garuda Sadashiva Rao was a tireless freedom fighter of Karnataka — a soldier of the Congress who gave up a settled life to serve the nation through the non-cooperation and civil disobedience movements. From his home in Udupi to the jails of the British, he spent his life in the service of the motherland.
overview: Born in 1882 near Udupi, Garuda Sadashiva Rao was drawn early to the national movement. He joined the Congress and threw himself into the campaigns that Gandhi led — the non-cooperation movement, the salt satyagraha, and the civil disobedience movement — organising the villages of the coastal Karnataka country for freedom.

He was arrested again and again for his work, spending years in British jails, and each release only returned him to the struggle with renewed energy. He worked for khadi, for prohibition, for the uplift of the villages, and for the unity of the nation — serving as a member of the Karnataka Congress and a trusted worker of the movement.

After independence, he continued to serve the people he had fought for, working for social reform and public welfare until his death in 1958. His life was the quiet, complete sacrifice of a worker of Bhārat — the kind of man on whose shoulders the freedom movement was really carried.

coreIdeas.title: The Congress Worker
coreIdeas.text: A dedicated soldier of the national movement.

coreIdeas.title: Gandhi's Campaigns
coreIdeas.text: Non-cooperation, salt satyagraha, civil disobedience.

coreIdeas.title: The Jail Years
coreIdeas.text: Arrested repeatedly, he served years in British prisons.

coreIdeas.title: The Village Worker
coreIdeas.text: Organising the villages of coastal Karnataka.

coreIdeas.title: Service After Freedom
coreIdeas.text: He kept serving the people after independence.

items.legacy: Garuda Sadashiva Rao is remembered in Karnataka as a complete freedom fighter — a man who gave his whole life to the nation without seeking any office or honour. His story is the story of the thousands of quiet workers of the Congress who built the freedom of Bhārat with their sacrifice.

items.name: Sushil Kumar Sen
items.tagline: The young revolutionary who defied the police as a boy of fifteen
items.attribution: Sushil Kumar Sen — a revolutionary of Bengal
items.quote: I am a son of Bhārat — and no terror can make me betray my land.
items.summary: Sushil Kumar Sen was a young revolutionary of Bengal whose defiance blazed early and ended early — he lived only twenty-three years. As a boy of fifteen he struck at a brutal British police officer; as a revolutionary he was captured and hanged, going to the gallows with the calm courage that made him a symbol of the armed youth of Bhārat.
overview: Born in Bengal in 1911, Sushil Kumar Sen grew up in the fiery years when the revolutionary movement was at its height. The official account of his life records that at fifteen, he taught a lesson to a British police officer who was mercilessly beating people — an act that marked the beginning of a short life of defiance.

He joined the revolutionary underground and took part in the movement's activities against the empire. Captured by the police, he was tried and sentenced to death — and the British, who had hoped for a confession, found in the young man only the calm of a patriot who had made his peace with death.

He was hanged in 1934, at the age of twenty-three. The account of his short life in the Bharata Bharati series ends with the words that he gave his life for his country without a moment's regret — one of the youngest of the revolutionaries to mount the gallows with a smile.

coreIdeas.title: The Boy Rebel
coreIdeas.text: He defied a brutal police officer at fifteen.

coreIdeas.title: The Underground
coreIdeas.text: He joined the revolutionary movement of Bengal.

coreIdeas.title: The Trial
coreIdeas.text: Condemned, he faced death without fear.

coreIdeas.title: The Gallows at Twenty-Three
coreIdeas.text: Hanged in 1934 for the freedom of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: The Calm Patriot
coreIdeas.text: He gave his life without a moment's regret.

items.legacy: Sushil Kumar Sen is remembered as one of the youngest martyrs of the revolutionary movement — a boy who gave his life before he could grow to manhood. His story, told to every generation in the Bharata Bharati series, remains a reminder of the terrible price paid by the youth of Bhārat for its freedom.

items.name: Purushottam Das Tandon
items.tagline: Rajarshi Tandon — the Gandhian leader of the Hindi heartland
items.attribution: Purushottam Das Tandon — 'Rajarshi'
items.quote: The village is the soul of Bhārat — her freedom means the freedom of her villages.
items.summary: Purushottam Das Tandon, honoured as Rajarshi — 'the kingly sage' — was a towering leader of the Congress from Uttar Pradesh, a Gandhian of unimpeachable integrity who gave his life to the freedom struggle and to the cause of Hindi. He served as Speaker of the assembly, led the Congress in the Hindi heartland, and was honoured with the Bharat Ratna.
overview: Born in Allahabad in 1882, Tandon was drawn to the national movement in his youth and became one of the earliest followers of Gandhi, serving as the secretary of the Allahabad Congress committee. He threw himself into the non-cooperation and civil disobedience movements, was arrested again and again, and became known for a simplicity and integrity that earned him the title Rajarshi.

He worked tirelessly for the villages and for the cause of Hindi — opposing the anglicisation of public life and insisting that the language of the people must be the language of the nation. He also played a leading role in the organisation of the Congress, serving as its president in 1950 and as the Speaker of the United Provinces assembly.

After independence, Tandon continued to serve as a member of the Constituent Assembly and the Lok Sabha, and in 1961 he received the Bharat Ratna, the highest honour of the republic. He died in 1962, remembered as a leader of unmatched purity of character — the sage-king of the Congress.

coreIdeas.title: Rajarshi
coreIdeas.text: 'The kingly sage' — a title earned by his integrity.

coreIdeas.title: The Gandhian
coreIdeas.text: A loyal follower of Gandhi and his methods.

coreIdeas.title: The Cause of Hindi
coreIdeas.text: He fought for the language of the common people.

coreIdeas.title: Congress President
coreIdeas.text: He led the party in 1950.

coreIdeas.title: Bharat Ratna
coreIdeas.text: The republic's highest honour, awarded in 1961.

items.legacy: Purushottam Das Tandon is remembered as one of the purest leaders of the freedom movement — a man whose life was as simple as his principles. His name is honoured in the Hindi heartland as the champion of the language and the villages of Bhārat, and his integrity remains a standard for public life.

items.name: Umakant Keshav Apte
items.tagline: The revolutionary who founded the Abhinav Bharat society
items.attribution: Umakant Keshav Apte
items.quote: What is a life worth that is not offered to the motherland?
items.summary: Umakant Keshav Apte was a fiery revolutionary of Maharashtra — a close associate of Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and a founder of the secret society Abhinav Bharat, which swore to win freedom by force. Hunted by the British for his part in revolutionary plots, he gave his life in 1915 while resisting arrest.
overview: Born in Maharashtra in 1881, Umakant Keshav Apte grew up in the atmosphere of Maharashtra's revolutionary nationalism, shaped by the memory of Shivaji and the writings of the age. He became a close associate of Savarkar and helped found Abhinav Bharat, the secret society dedicated to armed revolution against the British.

The society spread its nets across Maharashtra, training young men and preparing risings. When the British struck at the revolutionary movement, Apte was hunted relentlessly — and in 1915, cornered by the police, he chose death over capture, falling in the fight that ended his short, blazing life.

His death at thirty-four made him a martyr of the armed struggle — one of the many young men of Maharashtra who gave their lives in the years before Gandhi's mass movement. The revolutionary tradition he helped found became one of the streams that fed the freedom of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.text: The secret society he helped found for armed revolution.

coreIdeas.title: The Savarkar Circle

items.legacy: Umakant Keshav Apte is remembered as one of the founders of the revolutionary movement of Maharashtra — a man who gave his life rather than let the empire take him. His name stands in the roll of the martyrs of the armed struggle, honoured in the history of the freedom movement of Bhārat.

items.name: Surapura Venkatappa Nayaka
items.tagline: The prince of Surapura who died fighting the British in 1858
items.attribution: Venkatappa Nayaka — the Raja of Surapura
items.quote: I would rather die as a free prince than live as a servant of the company.
items.summary: Venkatappa Nayaka was the young prince of Surapura, a small principality in the north-east of Karnataka, whose rebellion in 1858 made him one of the last kings of Bhārat to fall fighting the British. Betrayed after a heroic resistance, the twenty-year-old prince was killed by the British — his death one of the final acts of the great uprising.
overview: Surapura was a small but proud principality in the Raichur country, ruled by a line of Nayaka chiefs. When the 1857 uprising swept Bhārat, its young prince Venkatappa — barely twenty years old — refused to submit to the British Resident and openly sided with the revolt, preparing his fort for war.

The British, alarmed by the rising in the Deccan, marched on Surapura in 1858. The young prince defended his fort with desperate courage, but treachery from within opened its gates; in the fighting that followed, Venkatappa was killed — by the official account, shot, and by the people's account, betrayed to his death rather than surrender.

His death marked the end of the last sparks of the 1857 uprising in the south — and the end of the old order of the small kingdoms of Karnataka. The people of the region never forgot their young prince, and today Venkatappa Nayaka is honoured across Karnataka as one of the last warrior-kings to die for the freedom of Bhārat.

items.legacy: Venkatappa Nayaka is honoured across Karnataka as a martyr of the first war of independence — the young prince who chose death over submission. His story, told in the Bharata Bharati series and remembered in the Raichur country, keeps alive the memory of the last warrior-kingdoms of the south.

items.name: Jatindra Mohan Sengupta
items.tagline: The firebrand of Bengal — Deshbandhu of the eastern province
items.attribution: Jatindra Mohan Sengupta
items.quote: I have given my life to Bhārat — what does the empire's prison matter to me?
items.summary: Jatindra Mohan Sengupta was a towering leader of Bengal — a barrister who gave up his practice to join Gandhi's movement, served as mayor of Calcutta, and led the freedom struggle with such fire that the people of East Bengal called him their Deshbandhu, 'friend of the country'. He died in 1933 while being taken to the Andamans, a martyr of the movement.
overview: Born in Chittagong in 1885, Sengupta trained as a barrister in England and returned to a brilliant legal career in Calcutta. But the national movement claimed him: he joined the Congress, and from 1921 he devoted himself wholly to the struggle, leading the non-cooperation movement in Bengal and serving as the mayor of Calcutta.

He was a fearless orator and organiser who led Bengal's civil disobedience campaigns, was arrested again and again, and served years in prison. His name became a rallying cry in East Bengal, where the people honoured him as Deshbandhu — and his leadership kept the fire of the movement burning in the province.

In 1933, already weakened by years in prison, he was ordered transported to the Andamans; on the way he fell ill and died. Bengal mourned him as a hero, and his funeral was one of the greatest the city had seen. He was the Deshbandhu of the east — the leader who gave everything for the freedom of Bhārat.

items.legacy: Jatindra Mohan Sengupta is remembered as one of the greatest leaders of Bengal — the Deshbandhu whose fire inspired the east. His name is honoured in the history of the Congress, his memory is cherished in Bengal and Bangladesh alike, and his life remains a model of the complete sacrifice of the freedom struggle.

items.name: Thimmappa Nayaka
items.tagline: The shepherd-chief who fought the empire in the southern hills
items.attribution: Thimmappa Nayaka — a hill chieftain of Karnataka
items.quote: The hills are free — and the man of the hills bows to no master.
items.summary: Thimmappa Nayaka was a hill chieftain of Karnataka who rose against the rule of the empire of his time — a leader of the shepherd and hill communities whose resistance made him a folk hero. His story, preserved in the Bharata Bharati series, tells of a warrior of the common people who defied the powerful and died for the freedom of his hills.
overview: The traditions of the Karnataka hills remember Thimmappa Nayaka as a chieftain of the shepherd community — a man of the forests and the hills who refused to bow to the tax-collectors and officials of the dominant power of the age. His defiance made him the champion of the poor hill folk.

His resistance grew into open revolt: Thimmappa Nayaka and his followers harried the forces sent against them, using the hills and forests that were their home as their fortress. For a time, the power of the region could not crush the shepherd-chief and his little army of the hills.

Eventually overwhelmed by superior forces, Thimmappa Nayaka was captured and put to death — but his name passed into the legends of the people. The Bharata Bharati series preserves his story as one of the many resisters of the common people of Bhārat who fought against foreign and feudal domination long before the modern freedom movement.

coreIdeas.text: His memory lives in the traditions of the people.

coreIdeas.title: Death for Freedom
coreIdeas.text: He gave his life rather than submit.

items.legacy: Thimmappa Nayaka is remembered as a hero of the common people of the Karnataka hills — one of the resisters whose stories the Bharata Bharati series preserves. His name is honoured in the folk memory of the region as a proof that the love of freedom burned in every village and every hill of Bhārat.

items.name: Lala Har Dayal
items.tagline: The firebrand who founded the Ghadar Party in America
items.attribution: Lala Har Dayal — the founder of the Ghadar movement
items.quote: Revolt, revolt, revolt — the freedom of Bhārat must be won by revolution.
items.quoteSource: The cry of the Ghadar movement
items.summary: Lala Har Dayal was a scholar and revolutionary who carried the cause of Bhārat's freedom across the world. In America he founded the Ghadar Party — 'the party of revolt' — which organised the emigrant workers of Bhārat to rise against the British, and his fiery writings and speeches made him one of the most hunted men of the empire.
overview: Born in Delhi in 1884, Har Dayal was a brilliant student who mastered Sanskrit and philosophy and studied at Oxford. But his heart was in the freedom of Bhārat, and he gave up scholarship for revolution, moving through the centres of the Indian diaspora and preaching revolt against the British.

In 1913 he founded the Ghadar Party in San Francisco — an organisation of the Punjabi workers and peasants of America and Canada who, remembering the humiliations of the empire, swore to free Bhārat by force. The party's newspaper, Ghadar, carried the cry of revolution to every household of the diaspora, and its members began to return to Bhārat to light the rising.

The British, terrified of Har Dayal's reach, had him pursued across the world; he fled to Europe and lived in exile, always working for Bhārat. He returned to India only in 1938, a year before his death, and died in 1939 — having given the freedom movement one of its most daring international organisers.

coreIdeas.title: The Ghadar Party
coreIdeas.text: The revolutionary party he founded in America in 1913.

coreIdeas.title: The Diaspora Rising
coreIdeas.text: He organised the workers of Bhārat abroad for revolt.

coreIdeas.title: The Ghadar Newspaper
coreIdeas.text: Its cry of revolution reached every emigrant home.

coreIdeas.title: The Hunted Exile
coreIdeas.text: The empire pursued him across the world.

coreIdeas.title: Revolution, Not Petition
coreIdeas.text: His unshakeable belief in armed revolt.

items.legacy: Lala Har Dayal is remembered as the founder of the Ghadar movement — the revolutionary who carried the freedom struggle of Bhārat to the far shores of America. His party's members returned to Bhārat to fight, his writings inspired a generation, and his name remains one of the great international chapters of the freedom movement.

items.name: Kasturba Gandhi
items.tagline: The silent strength behind the Mahatma — the mother of the nation
items.attribution: Kasturba Gandhi — the wife of Mahatma Gandhi
items.quote: I am not afraid of prison — the jail is the home of every true servant of Bhārat.
items.summary: Kasturba Gandhi was the wife and lifelong companion of the Mahatma — a woman of quiet iron who marched beside Gandhi through every struggle of his life, from South Africa to the Quit India movement. She went to prison, worked among the poor, and gave her life for the nation, dying in 1944 in the Aga Khan Palace while imprisoned with her husband.
overview: Born in 1869 in Porbandar and married to Mohandas Gandhi at thirteen, Kasturba was an unlettered village girl who grew, through a lifetime beside the Mahatma, into one of the great women of the freedom movement. She was his first pupil and his sternest critic — the one person who could argue with the Mahatma and hold her ground.

She followed him to South Africa, where she joined the satyagraha campaigns and went to prison for the rights of the people of Bhārat. Back in Bhārat, she marched in the salt satyagraha, worked for the uplift of women and the removal of untouchability, and served in the ashrams with the same simplicity as the humblest worker.

In 1942, both Gandhi and Kasturba were imprisoned in the Aga Khan Palace after the Quit India call. There, in 1944, her failing health gave way; Gandhi held her hand as she died, and the whole nation mourned the woman who had been, in his own words, his 'better half'. She was the mother of the nation in every sense.

coreIdeas.title: The Companion of the Mahatma
coreIdeas.text: Sixty-two years beside Gandhi through every struggle.

coreIdeas.title: The Satyagrahi
coreIdeas.text: She went to prison in South Africa and Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: The Social Worker
coreIdeas.text: She worked for women and against untouchability.

coreIdeas.title: The Quit India Prisoner
coreIdeas.text: Imprisoned with Gandhi in 1942.

coreIdeas.title: Death in Detention
coreIdeas.text: She died in the Aga Khan Palace in 1944.

items.legacy: Kasturba Gandhi is honoured as the mother of the nation — the woman whose quiet strength carried the Mahatma and whose sacrifice matched his own. Her memory is kept alive by the Kasturba trusts that work for rural women, and her life remains the proof that the freedom of Bhārat was built by its women as much as by its men.

items.name: Karnad Sadashiva Rao
items.tagline: The Gandhi of Karnataka — who gave his wealth and health to the nation
items.attribution: Karnad Sadashiva Rao
items.quote: Let me spend my all for the motherland — my money, my strength, and my life.
items.summary: Karnad Sadashiva Rao was one of the greatest workers of the Congress in Karnataka — a man of wealth who gave it all to the nation, and a leader whose name became synonymous with service. He spread Gandhi's message across the state, gave his fortune to the movement, and wore out his health in the cause — honoured as the Gandhi of Karnataka.
overview: Born in 1881, Karnad Sadashiva Rao inherited wealth and position — but the national movement claimed him early. He joined the Congress and became one of the most dedicated workers of Karnataka, travelling the length of the state to spread Gandhi's message of swaraj, khadi, and swadeshi.

His generosity was legendary: he donated his properties and his fortune to the Congress and to the causes of the people, gave freely for education and relief, and lived a life of austerity in the service of the nation. For his work he was arrested and imprisoned during the salt satyagraha and other campaigns.

The years of struggle wore down his health, and he died in 1937, at just fifty-six. Karnataka mourned a leader who had given everything — and his name remains honoured across the state as the very symbol of selfless service to the motherland.

coreIdeas.title: The Gandhi of Karnataka
coreIdeas.text: The title his people gave him for his service.

coreIdeas.title: The Generous Donor
coreIdeas.text: He gave his fortune to the freedom movement.

coreIdeas.title: The Congress Worker
coreIdeas.text: He spread the message of swaraj across Karnataka.

coreIdeas.title: The Prisoner
coreIdeas.text: Arrested during the salt satyagraha and campaigns.

coreIdeas.title: Service Unto Death
coreIdeas.text: He wore out his health in the nation's cause.

items.legacy: Karnad Sadashiva Rao is remembered across Karnataka as the very type of the selfless worker — a man who could have lived in ease but chose to give everything to the motherland. His name is honoured in the history of the Congress of the state, and his life remains the model of sacrifice for every worker of Bhārat.

items.name: Sampurnanand
items.tagline: The scholar-politician who governed Uttar Pradesh
items.attribution: Sampurnanand — scholar, freedom fighter, and Chief Minister
items.quote: Freedom without education is a lamp without oil — both must burn together.
items.summary: Sampurnanand was a scholar, a freedom fighter, and the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh — a leader of the Congress who joined the movement in its fiery years, went to prison for the nation, and then governed the largest state of Bhārat. He was also a profound scholar of Indian philosophy who wrote on the traditions of Bhārat.
overview: Born in Varanasi in 1891, Sampurnanand was a brilliant student of history and philosophy who was drawn to the national movement in his youth. He joined the Congress, took part in the non-cooperation and civil disobedience movements, and spent years in British prisons for the cause of freedom.

A scholar as well as a politician, he wrote extensively on Indian philosophy and culture, and his learning made him one of the most respected leaders of the Congress. After independence, he served as a minister in Uttar Pradesh and then, from 1954, as the state's Chief Minister for six years.

His government worked for education, land reform, and the uplift of the villages. He died in 1969, remembered as a leader of learning and integrity — the scholar who governed one of the great states of Bhārat with the mind of a teacher.

coreIdeas.title: The Scholar Patriot
coreIdeas.text: A student of history and philosophy who joined the struggle.

coreIdeas.title: The Prison Years
coreIdeas.text: He served time for the nation during the campaigns.

coreIdeas.title: The Writer
coreIdeas.text: He wrote deeply on the traditions of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: Chief Minister
coreIdeas.text: He governed Uttar Pradesh from 1954.

coreIdeas.title: Education and Reform
coreIdeas.text: His government worked for learning and the villages.

items.legacy: Sampurnanand is remembered as a leader who joined learning with politics — a freedom fighter who governed and taught with equal devotion. His books on Indian thought remain valued, his name is honoured in Uttar Pradesh, and his life shows the depth of the tradition of Bhārat within the freedom movement.

items.name: Janakidevi Bajaj
items.tagline: The devoted wife of Jamnalal Bajaj — a soldier of the freedom movement
items.attribution: Janakidevi Bajaj — the wife of Jamnalal Bajaj
items.quote: The freedom of Bhārat is my family's cause — and I will serve it with my whole heart.
items.summary: Janakidevi Bajaj was the wife of Jamnalal Bajaj, the great industrialist and close associate of Gandhi — and herself a devoted soldier of the freedom movement. She marched in the salt satyagraha, went to prison for the nation, and worked throughout her life for khadi, women's uplift, and the causes of the poor.
overview: Born in 1893 and married to Jamnalal Bajaj, the industrialist whom Gandhi called his fifth son, Janakidevi was drawn into the freedom movement by her husband's dedication. Together they became part of the innermost circle of Gandhi's ashram life at Wardha, and she took up the disciplines of the movement — khadi, simplicity, and service.

When the salt satyagraha came in 1930, Janakidevi marched and picketed, and she was arrested and imprisoned for the nation. Through the civil disobedience and Quit India movements she continued to serve — organising women, working for the removal of untouchability, and supporting the struggle with the resources of her family.

After independence, she continued the work of service and philanthropy, and in 1970 she was awarded the Padma Vibhushan for her contribution. She died in 1979, remembered as one of the great women of the freedom movement — the companion of one of its greatest servants.

coreIdeas.title: The Gandhian Household
coreIdeas.text: Her home at Wardha was the heart of the movement.

coreIdeas.title: The Salt Satyagrahi
coreIdeas.text: She marched and was arrested in 1930.

coreIdeas.title: The Prisoner
coreIdeas.text: She served imprisonment for the nation.

coreIdeas.title: The Organiser of Women
coreIdeas.text: She led women's work in the struggle.

coreIdeas.title: Padma Vibhushan
coreIdeas.text: The republic honoured her service in 1970.

items.legacy: Janakidevi Bajaj is remembered as one of the great women of the freedom movement — the companion of Jamnalal Bajaj who served the nation with her whole heart. Her name is honoured in the history of the movement, and her life remains an example of the families who gave everything for the freedom of Bhārat.

items.name: Motilal Ghosh
items.tagline: The fearless editor of the Amrita Bazar Patrika
items.attribution: Motilal Ghosh — journalist and patriot
items.quote: The pen is a weapon — and the truth is the ammunition of the patriot.
items.summary: Motilal Ghosh was one of the greatest journalists of the freedom struggle — the editor of the Amrita Bazar Patrika, the famous newspaper of Bengal, which he made a fearless voice against the empire. For fifty years he fought the British with the pen, exposing their injustices and championing the cause of the nation.
overview: Born in 1847, Motilal Ghosh joined the Amrita Bazar Patrika in its early days and, from 1872, edited it for fifty years, building it into one of the most powerful newspapers of Bhārat. The paper, founded by his brother Sisir Kumar Ghosh, became famous for its fearless criticism of the British government.

Ghosh used his paper to expose the injustices of the empire — the oppression of the indigo peasants, the misrule of officials, the attacks on the rights of the people. He was prosecuted and fined for his writings, but never silenced, and his paper remained the conscience of the nation through the most difficult decades of British rule.

He was also active in public life, serving on the Indian National Congress and championing the cause of the motherland till his death in 1922. The Amrita Bazar Patrika, under his hand, was the model of the patriotic press — and Motilal Ghosh its fearless editor.

coreIdeas.title: The Fearless Editor
coreIdeas.text: Fifty years at the head of the Amrita Bazar Patrika.

coreIdeas.title: The Pen as Weapon
coreIdeas.text: He used journalism to expose the empire's injustices.

coreIdeas.title: The Indigo Campaign
coreIdeas.text: His paper fought for the oppressed peasants.

coreIdeas.title: The Prosecuted Patriot
coreIdeas.text: Fined and prosecuted, but never silenced.

coreIdeas.title: The Conscience of the Nation
coreIdeas.text: His paper was the voice of the people.

items.legacy: Motilal Ghosh is remembered as one of the founders of the patriotic press of Bhārat — a journalist who proved that the pen could fight an empire. His Amrita Bazar Patrika remained a great voice of the nation for a century, and his name is honoured in the history of journalism of Bhārat.

items.name: G. Subramania Iyer
items.tagline: The founder of The Hindu — the voice of the South
items.attribution: G. Subramania Iyer — journalist and patriot
items.quote: A free people need a free press — the newspaper is the school of the citizen.
items.summary: G. Subramania Iyer was the founder of The Hindu, one of the greatest newspapers of the world, and a pioneer of the national movement in the South. A colleague of the early Congress leaders, he used his paper to awaken Madras to the cause of freedom, and his journalism helped build the national consciousness of the South.
overview: Born in 1855 in Madras, Subramania Iyer was a young lawyer drawn to public life. In 1878, with a group of patriot friends, he founded The Hindu — a weekly that grew into one of the world's great newspapers — to voice the grievances of the people and to advocate self-rule.

He was among the founders of the Indian National Congress in 1885 and served as one of its earliest secretaries, carrying the message of the movement across the South. Through The Hindu he educated the reading public of Madras on the politics of the nation, the evils of foreign rule, and the need for self-government.

He served on the Madras legislative council, where he fought for the rights of the people, and remained a voice of reason and patriotism till his death in 1916. His paper, The Hindu, grew into one of the most respected institutions of Bhārat — the living monument of its founder.

coreIdeas.title: The Founder of The Hindu
coreIdeas.text: The great newspaper he began in 1878.

coreIdeas.title: The Congress Pioneer
coreIdeas.text: Among the founders of the Indian National Congress.

coreIdeas.title: The Educator of the South
coreIdeas.text: He awakened Madras to the cause of freedom.

coreIdeas.title: The Legislator
coreIdeas.text: He fought for the people's rights in the council.

coreIdeas.title: The Free Press
coreIdeas.text: His paper became one of the world's greatest.

items.legacy: G. Subramania Iyer is remembered as the founder of The Hindu and a pioneer of the national movement in the South. His newspaper became one of the great institutions of the world, and his life remains an example of how journalism and patriotism can build a nation's consciousness.

items.name: S. Sadananda
items.tagline: The Gandhian worker who served the people of Karnataka
items.attribution: S. Sadananda — a freedom fighter of Karnataka
items.quote: Serve the motherland in the village — that is where the real Bhārat lives.
items.summary: S. Sadananda was a devoted freedom fighter and Gandhian of Karnataka who gave his life to the national movement and to the service of the villages. A worker of the Congress and of Gandhi's constructive programmes, he spent his life — and his years in prison — in the service of the motherland.
overview: Born in 1889 in the coastal country of Karnataka, Sadananda was drawn to the national movement in its early years and became one of the dedicated workers of the Congress in the region. He joined the campaigns of non-cooperation and civil disobedience, organising the people of the coastal districts for freedom.

He was arrested several times for his participation in the movement and served terms in British prisons, each time returning to the struggle with renewed devotion. He worked for khadi, for prohibition, for the uplift of the villages, and for the constructive programmes that Gandhi placed at the heart of the movement.

After independence, he continued to serve the people as a social worker, devoting his remaining years to the causes he had fought for. He died in 1970, remembered as one of the quiet, complete workers on whose shoulders the freedom movement of Karnataka was carried.

coreIdeas.title: The Congress Worker
coreIdeas.text: A dedicated soldier of the movement in coastal Karnataka.

coreIdeas.title: The Prison Years
coreIdeas.text: He served jail terms for the nation's cause.

coreIdeas.title: The Constructive Worker
coreIdeas.text: Khadi, prohibition, and village uplift were his work.

coreIdeas.title: The Gandhian
coreIdeas.text: He lived and worked by Gandhi's methods.

coreIdeas.title: Service After Freedom
coreIdeas.text: He kept serving the people till his death.

items.legacy: S. Sadananda is remembered in Karnataka as one of the selfless workers of the freedom movement — a man who asked nothing for himself and gave everything to the nation. His life is part of the great roll of the quiet soldiers of Bhārat's freedom.

items.name: Nani Baladevi
items.tagline: The fearless woman of Goa who defied the Portuguese in the freedom struggle
items.attribution: Nani Baladevi — a freedom fighter of Goa
items.quote: They filled my body with chillies — but they could not fill my heart with fear.
items.summary: Nani Baladevi was a fearless woman freedom fighter of Goa who rose against the Portuguese rulers of the territory. With little formal schooling but boundless courage, she joined the liberation struggle, went to prison for the motherland, and endured torture without ever betraying her comrades — a symbol of the women of Bhārat's indomitable spirit.
overview: Born in Goa when the territory was still under Portuguese rule, Nani Baladevi grew up in a land where freedom was denied and protest was punished. With only a little schooling, she understood the cause of the motherland and joined the movement for the liberation of Goa, serving the underground with total devotion.

She was arrested for her part in the struggle, and in prison the Portuguese authorities tortured her — the accounts of her life record that they stuffed her body with chilli powder — but she never revealed the secrets of the revolutionaries. Her courage under torture became the pride of the movement.

After Goa's liberation in 1961, she continued to serve the people and was honoured for her sacrifice. She died in 1997, remembered as the symbol of the self-respect and courage of the women of Bhārat — one who gave her body to pain but never her spirit to the enemy.

coreIdeas.text: She fought the Portuguese rulers of Goa.

coreIdeas.title: The Prisoner
coreIdeas.text: Arrested and jailed for the motherland.

coreIdeas.title: The Torture
coreIdeas.text: She endured torture without betraying her comrades.

coreIdeas.title: The Fearless Woman
coreIdeas.text: The symbol of the courage of the women of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: The Honoured Patriot

items.legacy: Nani Baladevi is remembered as one of the bravest women of the freedom struggle — the Goan who endured torture and prison for the motherland without a moment's fear. Her name is honoured in the history of Goa's liberation, and her courage remains the pride of the women of Bhārat.

items.name: B.R. Pantulu
items.tagline: The journalist and patriot of Andhra who fought for the nation
items.attribution: B.R. Pantulu — journalist and freedom fighter
items.quote: The motherland must be free — and the press of the motherland must say so.
items.summary: B.R. Pantulu was a journalist and patriot of Andhra who used his paper and his pen to serve the freedom movement. A fearless writer and organiser, he campaigned against foreign rule through his journalism, joined the national movement, and spent his life in the cause of the motherland.
overview: Born in Andhra in 1875, Pantulu was drawn to journalism and public life in his youth. He edited and published newspapers that spoke boldly for the people and against the injustices of the empire, building a reputation as a fearless writer of the region.

He joined the national movement and threw his paper and his energies into the struggle for freedom, campaigning for swaraj and for the rights of the people of Andhra. He worked with the Congress and with the leaders of the region, using the press as a weapon of the movement.

His life was one of unbroken service to the motherland, and he died in 1945 — two years before the freedom he had fought for. He is remembered in Andhra as one of the pioneers of its patriotic journalism and of its freedom struggle.

coreIdeas.title: The Journalist Patriot
coreIdeas.text: He used his papers to fight for the motherland.

coreIdeas.title: The Congress Worker
coreIdeas.text: He joined the national movement of the region.

coreIdeas.title: The Voice of Andhra
coreIdeas.text: His writing awakened the people of Andhra.

coreIdeas.title: The Fearless Writer

coreIdeas.title: Service to the End
coreIdeas.text: He served the cause till his death in 1945.

items.legacy: B.R. Pantulu is remembered in Andhra as a pioneer of patriotic journalism and of the freedom struggle of the region. His papers and his pen served the motherland for a lifetime, and his name is honoured in the history of the press and the movement of the South.

items.name: Prabhavati Devi
items.tagline: The wife of Jayaprakash Narayan — a dedicated Gandhian worker
items.attribution: Prabhavati Devi — the wife of Jayaprakash Narayan
items.quote: The home and the nation are one — a woman serves the motherland from both.
items.summary: Prabhavati Devi was the wife of Jayaprakash Narayan and herself a devoted Gandhian worker of the freedom movement. She marched in the campaigns, went to prison for the nation, and worked throughout her life for khadi, women's uplift, and the constructive programmes of the movement.
overview: Born in Bihar in 1906, Prabhavati Devi grew up in a family of the freedom movement and was married to Jayaprakash Narayan, the future hero of the struggle. She joined the Congress and took up the disciplines of Gandhian service, living a life of simplicity dedicated to the nation.

She took part in the salt satyagraha and the subsequent campaigns, and was arrested and imprisoned for her participation in the freedom movement. She worked for khadi and village industries, for the uplift of women, and for the removal of untouchability, serving in the constructive programmes that Gandhi placed at the centre of the struggle.

After independence, she continued her service to the people and stood beside her husband in his later movements for the reform of the nation. She died in 1973, remembered as one of the devoted women workers of the freedom movement — the companion of one of its greatest leaders.

coreIdeas.title: The Gandhian Worker
coreIdeas.text: She devoted herself to the constructive programmes.

coreIdeas.title: The Salt Satyagrahi
coreIdeas.text: She marched and was imprisoned for the nation.

coreIdeas.title: Women's Uplift
coreIdeas.text: She worked for the women of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: The Companion of JP
coreIdeas.text: She stood beside Jayaprakash Narayan throughout.

coreIdeas.title: Service Without End
coreIdeas.text: She served the people even after independence.

items.legacy: Prabhavati Devi is remembered as one of the devoted women of the freedom movement — a Gandhian worker who gave her life to the nation and stood beside one of its greatest leaders. Her name is honoured in the history of the movement of Bihar, and her service remains an example for the women of Bhārat.

items.name: Dinakar Desai
items.tagline: The freedom fighter and social worker of Karnataka
items.attribution: Dinakar Desai — freedom fighter and social worker
items.quote: Freedom is not a gift — it is a debt that every generation must repay with service.
items.summary: Dinakar Desai was a freedom fighter and social worker of Karnataka who served the nation through the movements of Gandhi and then devoted his life to the welfare of the people. He was imprisoned for his part in the freedom struggle and spent his later years in the service of the poor and the villages.
overview: Born in Karnataka in 1901, Dinakar Desai was drawn to the national movement in his youth and joined the campaigns of the Congress — the non-cooperation, civil disobedience, and Quit India movements. He organised the people of his region for freedom and suffered imprisonment for the cause.

His work was not limited to politics: he devoted himself to social service, working for the uplift of the villages, for education, and for the welfare of the poor. He served in the constructive programmes of the movement and continued this service after independence.
He died in 1982, remembered across Karnataka as a complete servant of the nation — a man who fought for freedom and then spent the rest of his life serving the people he had helped to free.

coreIdeas.text: He served in the campaigns of Gandhi's movement.

coreIdeas.title: The Prisoner
coreIdeas.text: Imprisoned for the cause of the motherland.

coreIdeas.title: The Social Worker
coreIdeas.text: He devoted his life to the uplift of the people.

coreIdeas.title: The Village Servant
coreIdeas.text: Education and welfare were his life's work.

coreIdeas.text: He kept serving the nation after independence.

items.legacy: Dinakar Desai is remembered in Karnataka as a freedom fighter who became a lifelong servant of the people — a man for whom freedom was only the beginning of the nation's work. His name is honoured in the history of the movement of the state, and his service remains an example of the complete patriot.

items.name: Gulzarilal Nanda
items.tagline: The labour leader who twice served as acting Prime Minister of Bhārat
items.attribution: Gulzarilal Nanda — economist, labour leader, and interim Prime Minister
items.quote: The worker is the maker of the nation — his rights are the rights of Bhārat itself.
items.summary: Gulzarilal Nanda was a freedom fighter, economist, and champion of labour who twice served as the acting Prime Minister of Bhārat — after the deaths of Nehru and Shastri. A scholar and a worker for the rights of the working people, he gave a lifetime of service to the nation he helped to free.
overview: Born in Sialkot in 1898, Nanda was a brilliant student of economics who joined the national movement in his youth. He worked with Gandhi and served in the labour movement, organising the workers and fighting for their rights — work that made him one of the leading labour leaders of the nation.

He served as a minister in the government of Bombay before independence and as the Labour Minister of independent Bhārat, where he championed the cause of the working people. He was a scholar of economics whose books and ideas influenced the planning of the nation.

In 1964, on the death of Nehru, he served as acting Prime Minister until Shastri's election, and again in 1966 after Shastri's death until Indira Gandhi took office. He died in 1998, at the age of a hundred years, honoured with the Bharat Ratna — a life of a century devoted to the nation.

coreIdeas.title: The Labour Leader
coreIdeas.text: A lifetime champion of the working people.

coreIdeas.title: The Economist
coreIdeas.text: His scholarship shaped the nation's planning.

coreIdeas.title: Acting Prime Minister
coreIdeas.text: He headed the nation twice in moments of crisis.

coreIdeas.title: The Freedom Fighter
coreIdeas.text: He served the movement of Gandhi.

coreIdeas.title: A Century of Service
coreIdeas.text: He lived a hundred years and served Bhārat all of them.

items.legacy: Gulzarilal Nanda is remembered as a leader of integrity and scholarship — the labour leader who steadied the nation in its moments of transition and served Bhārat for a full century. His Bharat Ratna and his name are honoured in the history of the republic as a symbol of service without ambition.

items.name: Pandit Taranath
items.tagline: The educationist who awakened the North — the pioneer of the Gurukula
items.attribution: Pandit Taranath — educationist and freedom fighter
items.quote: Education is the foundation of freedom — teach the child of Bhārat to stand tall.
items.summary: Pandit Taranath was an educationist and freedom fighter of Karnataka who believed that the freedom of Bhārat must begin in the classroom. He founded the famous Gurukula at Kapani, near Dharwad, where students were taught in the ancient way — in the open air, by the light of the vedas and the love of the motherland.
overview: Born in 1891, Pandit Taranath was a scholar and teacher who was deeply troubled by the anglicised education of the time, which made the children of Bhārat strangers to their own land. He believed that true freedom required an education rooted in the culture of Bhārat.

In 1921 he founded the Gurukula at Kapani, near Dharwad — a school in the ancient style, where students lived with their teacher, studied the scriptures and the classics of Bhārat, and were trained in body and mind together. The Gurukula became a centre of national education, drawing students and teachers devoted to the ideal of a free Bhārat.

His school was also a centre of the freedom movement, and Taranath himself was arrested for his nationalism. He died in 1943, but his Gurukula continued the work he had begun — the education of the children of Bhārat in the spirit of their own civilisation.
