items.legacy: Kharavela is honoured as the greatest king of ancient Odisha, and his Hathigumpha inscription is a national treasure. He is remembered as the proof that Kalinga could be conquered but never broken — and rose again to greatness.

items.name: Vishnuvardhana
items.tagline: The Hoysala emperor who raised Belur and Halebidu
items.attribution: The greatest of the Hoysala kings
items.quote: Let the stone speak — and let it speak of the gods.
items.summary: Vishnuvardhana was the greatest king of the Hoysala dynasty — the emperor who expanded his small kingdom into a power of the Deccan and raised the temples of Belur and Halebidu, the masterpieces of sculpture of Bhārat. Under his rule, Hoysala art reached the perfection that still draws the world to Karnataka.
overview: Ascending the Hoysala throne around 1108, Vishnuvardhana turned his kingdom — centred in the hills of southern Karnataka — into a major power. He campaigned against the neighbouring Chalukyas and Pandyas, extended his rule across the Deccan, and took the title 'emperor of the south'.

His greatest legacy is art: he built the Chennakesava temple at Belur, its walls covered with a profusion of sculpture that has no equal in Bhārat, and the magnificent Hoysaleshwara temple at Halebidu, carved with a thousand images of gods, dancers, and demons in stone so detailed it seems alive. The temples he raised are the summit of the Hoysala style, and UNESCO has placed them on the world heritage list.

He was a Jain by birth who converted to the Vaishnava faith under the influence of the saint Ramanuja, who visited his court. He died in 1152, leaving a kingdom of power and a legacy of beauty — and his capital Halebidu remains one of the greatest art galleries of the world in stone.

coreIdeas.title: The Empire Builder
coreIdeas.text: He made Hoysala power the master of the Deccan.

coreIdeas.title: Belur
coreIdeas.text: The Chennakesava temple — a summit of sculpture.

coreIdeas.title: Halebidu
coreIdeas.text: The Hoysaleshwara temple's thousand carved gods.

coreIdeas.title: The Convert
coreIdeas.text: Ramanuja's influence turned him to Vaishnavism.

coreIdeas.title: The World Heritage
coreIdeas.text: His temples now bear UNESCO's honour.

items.legacy: Vishnuvardhana is remembered as the king who made Karnataka's hills speak in stone. His temples of Belur and Halebidu are among the finest monuments of Bhārat, and his name stands at the head of the Hoysala golden age.

items.name: Nrupatunga
items.tagline: The Rashtrakuta emperor — patron of the first Kannada poetry
items.attribution: Amoghavarsha — the Rashtrakuta emperor
items.quote: The poet's song is the empire's best monument.
items.summary: Amoghavarsha Nrupatunga was the greatest emperor of the Rashtrakuta dynasty — the ruler of a vast Deccan empire who was also a poet and the patron of the first great work of Kannada literature, the Kavirajamarga. His long reign of over sixty years was an age of peace, art, and learning.
overview: Amoghavarsha ascended the Rashtrakuta throne in the early ninth century and ruled for over sixty years from the capital Manyakheta, in present-day Karnataka. His empire stretched across the Deccan, and his long, peaceful reign made it one of the richest states of the age — visited by traders and ambassadors from Arabia and Persia.

He was a poet-emperor: he is credited with a part of the Kavirajamarga, the first extant work of literary criticism in the Kannada language, which declares Kannada to be a great language 'between the Kaveri and the Godavari'. He was a devout patron of the Jain faith and of the scholars of every religion of his realm.

The crowning work of his dynasty's patronage was the great Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single rock, which reached its glory under his house. He is remembered as the gentle emperor — a Jain king who ruled with justice, wrote poetry, and gave his people a golden age.

coreIdeas.title: The Sixty-Year Reign
coreIdeas.text: One of the longest and most peaceful reigns in history of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: The Kavirajamarga
coreIdeas.text: He patronised the first classic of Kannada literature.

coreIdeas.title: Manyakheta
coreIdeas.text: His capital was a centre of trade and learning.

coreIdeas.title: The Poet-Emperor
coreIdeas.text: A king who wrote and judged poetry.

coreIdeas.title: The Jain Patron
coreIdeas.text: A Jain emperor of tolerance and justice.

items.legacy: Amoghavarsha Nrupatunga is honoured in Karnataka as the emperor who gave the Kannada language its first classic. His name is remembered wherever Kannada is spoken, and his reign is the golden age of the Rashtrakutas.

items.name: Shivappa Nayaka
items.tagline: The Keladi king who made Karnataka's farmers prosper
items.attribution: The king of Keladi
items.quote: A kingdom is measured not by its forts but by the fullness of its granaries.
items.summary: Shivappa Nayaka was the great king of Keladi in Karnataka — a ruler remembered above all for the 'Shivappa Nayaka system' of land revenue, a scientific and just system of taxation that made his kingdom's farmers prosper and his state the envy of the Deccan. He is the model of the good administrator-king.
overview: Shivappa Nayaka came to the throne of Keladi, the small but strategically placed kingdom of the Malnad hills, in the mid-seventeenth century. Though his reign was brief, he expanded his territory and, more importantly, reformed its economy with a precision that made him famous.

His land-revenue system is a classic of administration of Bhārat: a scientific survey of soils, classified by fertility, with taxes graded by the crop and the quality of the land — a 'fair and final' settlement that encouraged cultivation and filled the state's granaries without oppressing the farmer. The system was later praised and studied by the British.

He was a just and tolerant king, a patron of both the Hindu temples and the Jain and Muslim communities of his land. He died in 1660, and his successors, including the brave queen Chennamma, carried on his line — but it is his revenue system that made his name immortal in the history of governance of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: The Revenue System
coreIdeas.text: His scientific taxation made farmers prosper.

coreIdeas.title: The Soil Survey
coreIdeas.text: He classified land by fertility for fair taxes.

coreIdeas.title: The Good Administrator
coreIdeas.text: The model of the just and efficient king.

coreIdeas.title: The Tolerant Ruler
coreIdeas.text: He patronised every community of his land.

coreIdeas.title: The Keladi Legacy
coreIdeas.text: His line included the brave Chennamma.

items.legacy: Shivappa Nayaka is remembered as the ideal administrator-king of Karnataka, and his revenue system is still studied in economic history of Bhārat. He is the proof that the greatest king is not the one who conquers most, but the one who feeds his people best.

items.name: Keladi Chennamma
items.tagline: The queen who sheltered the child of Shivaji
items.attribution: The queen of Keladi
items.quote: I bend to no emperor — but I open my gates to the hunted.
items.summary: Keladi Chennamma was the brave queen of the small kingdom of Keladi in Karnataka who defied the might of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb — sheltering Rajaram, the son of Shivaji, when he fled the Mughal armies in 1689. Her defiance cost her a war with the empire, which she fought with skill and courage.
overview: Chennamma ruled the hill kingdom of Keladi, succeeding her husband, and proved herself a queen of unusual ability — an administrator who managed her small state with prudence and a warrior who was not afraid to fight. Her moment of history came in 1689, when the Mughal armies of Aurangzeb were hunting the family of Shivaji across Bhārat.

When Rajaram, the young son of Shivaji, fled south with the Mughals in pursuit, he sought refuge in Keladi. Chennamma sheltered him and sent him on with an escort — an act of defiance that Aurangzeb could not forgive. The emperor sent a great army against the tiny kingdom, but the queen's forces held their hill passes and fought the Mughals to a standstill.

The war with the empire was eventually settled, and Chennamma emerged with her kingdom intact and her honour untarnished. She died in 1697, and she is remembered as the queen who risked everything for dharma and for the family of the Maratha hero — a warrior queen of the same temper as Rani Lakshmibai and Rani Abbakka.

coreIdeas.title: The Refuge
coreIdeas.text: She sheltered Rajaram from the Mughal armies.

coreIdeas.title: The Defiance
coreIdeas.text: She refused to bow to Aurangzeb's might.

coreIdeas.title: The Hill War
coreIdeas.text: Her forces held the passes against the empire.

coreIdeas.title: The Queen-Administrator
coreIdeas.text: She ruled Keladi with prudence and strength.

coreIdeas.title: The Warrior Queen
coreIdeas.text: A heroine of the same temper as Lakshmibai.

items.legacy: Keladi Chennamma is honoured in Karnataka as one of its bravest queens, and her story is told with the other warrior women of the Deccan. She is the proof that courage is not measured by the size of the kingdom.

items.name: Rani Abbakka
items.tagline: The first woman to fight the Portuguese — and defeat them
items.attribution: The queen of Ullal
items.quote: The sea belongs to my people — and I will defend it with my life.
items.summary: Rani Abbakka was the queen of Ullal, on the coast of Karnataka, who fought the Portuguese for four decades in the sixteenth century — the first woman to lead of Bhārat a resistance against the European colonisers and one of the few rulers who repeatedly defeated them. She is honoured as the 'unconquered queen'.
overview: Abbakka was the queen of the small coastal kingdom of Ullal, near Mangalore, in the mid-sixteenth century. The Portuguese, masters of the sea, demanded tribute and control of the spice trade — and Abbakka refused. She allied with the neighbouring kingdoms and the Zamorin of Calicut, and she prepared her people for war.

When the Portuguese attacked Ullal, the queen led her forces personally, using the coastal terrain and the tides against the invaders. She defeated them repeatedly — in the battles of 1568 and 1571, the Portuguese generals were killed or driven back, and the queen's name became a terror to Goa. Her kingdom remained free when most of the coast had submitted.

She was finally betrayed and captured in a surprise attack and died in captivity around 1580 — but she was never conquered in battle. Her resistance is honoured as the first great stand of a ruler of Bhārat against European colonialism, and she is remembered as the queen who chose war with the empire rather than submission.

coreIdeas.title: The First Resister
coreIdeas.text: The first queen to fight of Bhārat the Portuguese.

coreIdeas.title: The Unconquered
coreIdeas.text: She was never defeated in open battle.

coreIdeas.title: The Sea Queen
coreIdeas.text: She used the tides and the coast as weapons.

coreIdeas.title: The Alliance
coreIdeas.text: She united the coast against the colonisers.

coreIdeas.title: The Betrayal
coreIdeas.text: Captured by treachery, not by battle.

items.legacy: Rani Abbakka is honoured in Karnataka with statues, a naval ship named for her, and a postal stamp — and her anniversary is observed as a day of homage to the warrior queen. She is the first name in the long roll of Bhārat's resistance to European conquest.

items.name: Rani Durgavati
items.tagline: The queen who fought the Mughal emperor — and fell fighting
items.attribution: The queen of Gondwana
items.quote: I am the queen of the Gonds — and I die fighting, not fleeing.
items.summary: Rani Durgavati was the queen of the Gond kingdom of Garha-Katanga in central Bhārat — a warrior-queen who ruled with skill after her husband's death and led her armies personally against the Mughal emperor Akbar's general Asaf Khan in 1564. She fell fighting, choosing death over surrender, and is honoured as one of Bhārat's greatest warrior queens.
overview: Born a princess of the Chandela dynasty in 1524, Durgavati was married to the Gond king Dalpat Shah of Garha-Katanga. When her husband died, she ruled as regent for her young son — and proved herself an exceptional queen, expanding her kingdom, building forts and tanks, and maintaining a well-trained army including war elephants.

In 1564, the Mughal emperor Akbar sent his general Asaf Khan with a great army to annex the rich Gond kingdom. The Rani, though outnumbered, chose to fight. She led her forces personally, and in the first encounter near Damoh she drove back the Mughal vanguard — but her army, facing reinforcements, was overwhelmed.

Wounded in the battle, she refused to retreat, saying she would rather die than yield. She took her own life with a dagger rather than be captured — and the Mughals, who admired valour even in enemies, built a memorial to her. She was forty, and her story became a legend of the struggle of the smaller kingdoms against the empire.

coreIdeas.title: The Queen-Regent
coreIdeas.text: She ruled and expanded the Gond kingdom.

coreIdeas.title: The 1564 War
coreIdeas.text: She fought Akbar's general to the last.

coreIdeas.title: The First Victory
coreIdeas.text: She drove back the Mughal vanguard at Damoh.

coreIdeas.title: Death Over Surrender
coreIdeas.text: She chose the dagger over captivity.

coreIdeas.title: The Warrior Ideal
coreIdeas.text: Honoured as one of Bhārat's bravest queens.

items.legacy: Rani Durgavati is honoured with her statue in the Indian Parliament complex and with the Rani Durgavati University of Jabalpur. Her birthday, 5 October, is observed in Madhya Pradesh as a day of homage to the queen who fell fighting the empire.

items.name: Jijabai
items.tagline: The mother who shaped Shivaji — the iron soul of the Maratha state
items.attribution: The mother of Chhatrapati Shivaji
items.region: Jijau's court at Shivneri and Raigad
items.quote: The kingdom of my son shall be the kingdom of the gods — I have sworn it.
items.summary: Jijabai was the mother of Chhatrapati Shivaji and the true architect of his spirit — the Rajput princess who raised her son in a land under Mughal rule, filling him with the stories of the epics and the dream of a Hindu swaraj. Her name, Jijau, is revered in Maharashtra as the mother who gave Bhārat its greatest hero.
overview: Born in 1598 into the Jadhav family of Sindkhed Raja, Jijabai was married to Shahaji Bhosale, a Maratha general in service of the Deccan sultanates. When her son Shivaji was born at Shivneri fort in 1630, she took charge of his education herself — raising him on the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, on tales of the ancient kings, and on the dream that one day the Marathas would rule their own land.

While her husband served the sultans of Bijapur and the Mughals, Jijabai remained the soul of the family's lands, guiding Shivaji from boyhood through the first daring acts of his career — the capture of forts, the establishment of a free kingdom, and the defiance of the Bijapur court. It was she who strengthened him for the great mission: Hindavi Swarajya, self-rule of the Hindus.

She lived to see her son crowned Chhatrapati in 1674 — and died shortly after, at Raigad. Her death at the moment of his triumph was mourned across Maharashtra, and she is remembered as Jijau — the mother whose stories, discipline, and iron will built the man who built the Maratha empire.

coreIdeas.title: The Mother of Shivaji
coreIdeas.text: She raised the founder of the Maratha state.

coreIdeas.title: The Epic Education
coreIdeas.text: Her son learned dharma from her stories.

coreIdeas.title: The Iron Will
coreIdeas.text: She gave Shivaji his courage and his mission.

coreIdeas.title: Hindavi Swarajya
coreIdeas.text: The dream of self-rule she planted in him.

coreIdeas.title: Jijau
coreIdeas.text: The name Maharashtra reveres with love.

items.legacy: Jijabai is honoured across Maharashtra, where her story is told in every school and her name given to institutions and roads. She is the proof that the greatest empires are first built in a mother's stories — and that behind every hero stands a mother with a dream.

items.name: Chhatrasal
items.tagline: The Bundela king who defied the Mughal empire
items.attribution: The founder of the Panna kingdom
items.quote: I will have my kingdom — or my shroud. I will not serve.
items.summary: Chhatrasal was the Bundela Rajput king who defied the Mughal empire for decades — carving out his own kingdom of Bundelkhand and defending it against three Mughal emperors. He was rescued at the end by the Maratha hero Bajirao I, and his friendship with the Peshwa sealed the alliance of the Rajputs and the Marathas.
overview: Born in 1649 into the Bundela clan, Chhatrasal grew up at the court of the Mughals, where his family served — but he dreamed of his own kingdom. At twenty-two he left the Mughal service, gathered a band of Bundela warriors, and began the war of independence of Bundelkhand against the empire of Aurangzeb.

For over three decades he fought and built: capturing forts, setting up his capital at Panna, and ruling a kingdom that stretched across Bundelkhand. He faced the armies of Aurangzeb and his successors, and though his kingdom was small, his guerrilla warfare and his alliances kept it alive against the greatest empire of the age.

In 1729, hard pressed by a Mughal general, Chhatrasal summoned the Maratha Peshwa Bajirao I, who marched to his rescue and defeated the Mughals. In gratitude, the dying king gave Bajirao a third of his kingdom and his daughter in marriage — and the alliance of the Bundelas and Marathas became part of the history of both houses. Chhatrasal died in 1731, his kingdom secure.

coreIdeas.title: The Independent Kingdom
coreIdeas.text: He founded the state of Panna in Bundelkhand.

coreIdeas.title: The Long Defiance
coreIdeas.text: Decades of war against three Mughal emperors.

coreIdeas.title: The Guerrilla King
coreIdeas.text: His hill warfare kept the empire at bay.

coreIdeas.title: The Bajirao Alliance
coreIdeas.text: The Peshwa rescued him in 1729.

coreIdeas.title: The Gift
coreIdeas.text: He gave Bajirao a third of his kingdom.

items.legacy: Chhatrasal is honoured in Bundelkhand as the king who refused to bow, and his legacy lives in the friendship of the Rajput and Maratha houses. His story is the classic tale of the small kingdom that defied the empire — and won.

items.name: Peshwa Baji Rao I
items.tagline: The sword of the Marathas — 'never has a spear been hurled like his'
items.attribution: The greatest of the Maratha Peshwas
items.quote: Shall we sit contentedly in the Deccan while the empire of the north is in ruin? Strike!
items.quoteSource: Baji Rao to the Maratha council
items.summary: Baji Rao I was the greatest of the Maratha Peshwas — the twenty-year-old who convinced the Maratha council to carry their banners beyond the Deccan, and who in twenty years of campaigning shattered the Mughal power in the north. The Mughal court itself said of him: 'never has a spear been hurled like his'.
overview: Baji Rao was raised by his father, the first Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath, in the arts of war and statecraft. When his father died in 1720, the twenty-year-old Baji Rao persuaded the Maratha king Shahu to appoint him Peshwa — and immediately argued for the great policy: the Marathas must go north, for the Mughal empire was decaying and the field was open.

In the campaigns that followed — over twenty years and dozens of battles — Baji Rao crossed the Narmada, defeated the Nizam, and carried the Maratha flags from Gujarat to Bengal, from Delhi's environs to the coast. His cavalry moved with a speed that left his enemies breathless, and the Mughal capital itself felt his shadow.

He died suddenly in 1740, at just forty, on campaign with his beloved Mastani. His son, the third Peshwa, extended the Maratha power to its zenith — but it was Baji Rao who had won the empire its destiny, and the Maratha historian Grant Duff called his era the age of the Maratha hero.

coreIdeas.title: The Northern Policy
coreIdeas.text: He carried the Marathas beyond the Deccan.

coreIdeas.title: The Blazing Cavalry
coreIdeas.text: Speed of movement that left empires helpless.

coreIdeas.title: The Nizam's Defeat
coreIdeas.text: He broke the power that threatened the Marathas.

coreIdeas.title: The Twenty Years
coreIdeas.text: A career of almost constant victory.

coreIdeas.title: The Legend
coreIdeas.text: The Mughal court feared his spear above all.

items.legacy: Baji Rao is honoured as the greatest warrior of the Maratha age, and his exploits fill the ballads of Maharashtra. His story — the young general who changed the destiny of a nation — is among the most stirring in history of Bhārat.

items.name: Rana Sanga
items.tagline: The Rajput emperor who fought Babur — and fought on with eighty wounds
items.attribution: The ruler of Mewar
items.quote: A Rajput does not count his wounds — he counts his enemies.
items.summary: Rana Sanga was the greatest Rajput ruler of his age — the emperor of Mewar who united the Rajput clans, defeated the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat, and was the last great power to face Babur, the founder of the Mughal empire, at the battle of Khanwa in 1527. He fought his wars with eighty wounds on his body and one arm lost.
overview: Sanga succeeded to the throne of Mewar in 1509 after a life of extraordinary suffering: as a young prince he had been imprisoned, poisoned, and maimed — losing an eye and an arm — yet he emerged with a will of iron. He rebuilt Mewar's power and, in a series of campaigns, defeated the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat, taking the title of emperor of the Rajputs.

When Babur, fresh from his conquest of Delhi, advanced, Sanga gathered the largest Rajput confederacy in history — the forces of Mewar, Marwar, Amber, and the allied clans. At Khanwa in 1527, the Rajput cavalry charged the Mughal guns with suicidal courage, but the artillery and tactics of Babur prevailed, and the Rajput cause was broken.

Sanga, who had fought at the head of his army, escaped the field but died within the year — tradition says of his wounds and of the poisoned cup of a trusted ally. He is remembered as the last great emperor of the Rajputs before the Mughal consolidation — the king whose eighty wounds told the story of a life of war.

coreIdeas.title: The Rajput Emperor
coreIdeas.text: He united the clans of Mewar and beyond.

coreIdeas.title: The Wounded Warrior
coreIdeas.text: Eighty wounds and a lost arm — and still he fought.

coreIdeas.title: Khanwa, 1527
coreIdeas.text: His great charge against Babur's guns.

coreIdeas.title: The Last Stand
coreIdeas.text: The final great Rajput power before the Mughals.

coreIdeas.title: The Defeats of the Sultans
coreIdeas.text: He broke Malwa and Gujarat in his prime.

items.legacy: Rana Sanga is honoured in Rajasthan as the emperor who carried Rajput pride to its last great height. His courage at Khanwa — riding against cannon with a sword — remains the Rajput ideal of honour.

items.name: Maharana Pratap
items.tagline: The king who never bowed — even when he lost everything
items.attribution: The ruler of Mewar
items.quote: The day shall come when I shall die fighting for Mewar — but never shall I bow.
items.summary: Maharana Pratap was the Rajput king of Mewar who refused to submit to the Mughal emperor Akbar — and who, after losing his capital and his kingdom, fought on from the hills for years until he won back his land. His battle with Man Singh at Haldighati in 1576 and his beloved horse Chetak are legends of valour of Bhārat.
overview: When Akbar demanded the submission of Mewar, the other Rajput houses had made peace with the empire — but Pratap, crowned in 1572, refused. He prepared for war instead, and in 1576 the Mughal army under Man Singh met him at the pass of Haldighati.

The battle of Haldighati was one of the most desperate of history of Bhārat: Pratap's outnumbered Rajputs charged the Mughal centre, and he himself attacked Man Singh's position — but his horse Chetak was wounded and the day was lost. The king escaped into the hills, and for years he lived in the wilderness, eating forest roots, while the Mughals held his capital.

Through years of guerrilla war he slowly rebuilt, winning back fort after fort — including the great fort of Kumbhalgarh — until Mewar was free again, and Akbar never conquered it. He died in 1597 of a hunting injury, having kept his word: he had never bowed. His son submitted to the Mughals after his death, but Pratap's refusal remains the eternal symbol of Rajput independence.

coreIdeas.title: The Refusal
coreIdeas.text: He defied Akbar when all others submitted.

coreIdeas.title: Haldighati, 1576
coreIdeas.text: The desperate charge against the Mughal army.

coreIdeas.title: Chetak
coreIdeas.text: His horse carried him to safety, wounded unto death.

coreIdeas.title: The Wilderness Years
coreIdeas.text: He lived in the hills and never surrendered.

coreIdeas.title: The Victory
coreIdeas.text: He won Mewar back — the unconquered kingdom.

items.legacy: Maharana Pratap is honoured across Rajasthan and Bhārat as the king who chose everything over submission. His story — and Chetak's — is sung in every Rajput home, and his refusal to bow is taught to every child as the meaning of self-respect.

items.name: Hakka & Bukka
items.tagline: The brothers who founded the Vijayanagara empire
items.attribution: Harihara and Bukka — founders of Vijayanagara
items.quote: The city of victory shall rise where the dharma of the land is reborn.
items.summary: Harihara and Bukka — Hakka and Bukka — were the brothers who founded the Vijayanagara empire in 1336, the great Hindu state that defended southern Bhārat for three centuries. Guided by the sage Vidyaranya, they built their capital at Hampi, whose ruins still astonish the world, and their dynasty became the shield of the south.
overview: In the early fourteenth century, the south of Bhārat had been ravaged by the armies of the Delhi Sultanate, and the old kingdoms had fallen. The brothers Harihara and Bukka, warriors of the Hoysala country, rose to rebuild — and tradition says they were guided by the sage Vidyaranya of Sringeri, who blessed the founding of a new kingdom that would restore Hindu rule.

In 1336 they founded Vijayanagara — the city of victory — on the banks of the Tungabhadra, in the boulder-strewn land of Hampi. From this capital their empire grew across the Deccan, defeating the sultanates and sheltering the temples, the Sanskrit learning, and the arts of the south.

Harihara ruled first, and Bukka succeeded him — and under their line, the empire became the wonder of travellers from Persia, Portugal, and China, who described a city of diamonds, temples, and bazaars richer than any in Europe. The brothers built the foundation of the greatest Hindu state of the age, and their empire survived for over three hundred years.

coreIdeas.title: The Founding
coreIdeas.text: They established Vijayanagara in 1336.

coreIdeas.title: The Two Brothers
coreIdeas.text: Harihara and Bukka ruled in succession.

coreIdeas.title: The Sage's Blessing
coreIdeas.text: Vidyaranya guided the empire's birth.

coreIdeas.title: The Shield of the South
coreIdeas.text: They protected Hindu culture for centuries.

coreIdeas.title: Hampi
coreIdeas.text: Their capital is a world heritage wonder.

items.legacy: Hakka and Bukka are honoured as the founders of the greatest empire of the Deccan, and their Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Their story — two brothers who raised a city of victory from the ruins of an age — is the founding legend of South Bhārat history.

items.name: Echchama Nayaka
items.tagline: The hill chieftain of the Keladi wars
items.attribution: The Nayaka of the Malnad hills
items.quote: The hills are my fort — and no army has ever taken a hill it cannot climb.
items.summary: Echchama Nayaka was a chieftain of the Malnad hills of Karnataka who is remembered in the traditions of the Keladi kingdom — a warrior of the hill country whose life was woven into the wars and legends of the region's seventeenth-century history.
overview: The Malnad — the wet hill country of Karnataka — was a land of small Nayaka chieftains and strong hill forts, of which Keladi was the greatest. Echchama Nayaka belonged to this world of hill warriors, whose alliances and rivalries shaped the politics of the region in the age of the Nayakas.

The traditions that remember him place him in the service and wars of the Keladi kingdom, a loyal and formidable warrior whose knowledge of the hills made him a valuable commander in the region's campaigns against the neighbouring powers, including the sultanates of the coast and the Bijapur kingdom.

He is remembered in the chronicles of the Keladi house as a warrior of courage and loyalty — one of the many Nayaka commanders whose swords built and defended the hill kingdom through its golden age. His name is preserved in the region's historical memory as a representative of the fierce independence of the Malnad warriors.

coreIdeas.title: The Hill Warrior
coreIdeas.text: A commander of the Malnad's fierce warrior clans.

coreIdeas.title: The Keladi Wars
coreIdeas.text: He served the hill kingdom's campaigns.

coreIdeas.title: The Fort Country
coreIdeas.text: His world was a land of hill forts and passes.

coreIdeas.title: The Loyal Commander
coreIdeas.text: Remembered for courage and service.

coreIdeas.title: The Malnad Spirit
coreIdeas.text: A symbol of the hill country's independence.

items.legacy: Echchama Nayaka is remembered in the chronicles of the Keladi kingdom as one of the brave Nayakas of the hill country. His story represents the countless warriors of the Malnad whose names survive in the region's traditions.

items.name: Bajiprabhu Deshpande
items.tagline: The warrior who held the pass at Pavan Khind
items.attribution: The Maratha warrior of Shivaji
items.quote: Hold the pass — hold the pass, whatever it costs.
items.summary: Bajiprabhu Deshpande was the Maratha warrior who held the mountain pass of Pavan Khind against a vast army, so that Shivaji could escape — and died fighting at the head of his men. His name is the Maratha ideal of sacrifice: the man who held the gate while his king rode to freedom.
overview: In 1660, Shivaji and his forces were surrounded at the fort of Panhala by the army of the Bijapur sultanate, led by the general Siddi Jauhar. Shivaji planned a daring escape, and the warrior Bajiprabhu Deshpande was given the rearguard: to hold the narrow pass of Pavan Khind until the king was safe.

Bajiprabhu and his band of Marathas stood in the pass against the entire Bijapur army. For hours they held the defile, fighting without rest, as the enemy hurled wave after wave against them. When Bajiprabhu fell, his brother and his comrades closed ranks and held the pass still — until word came that Shivaji had reached safety, and the Marathas fell back, having given their lives.

The stand of Pavan Khind is the most celebrated rearguard action in military history of Bhārat. Bajiprabhu's body, carried from the field, was honoured by Shivaji himself, and the pass where he died is still called the pass of sacrifice — a monument to the warrior who held the gate.

coreIdeas.text: The pass he held while his king escaped.

coreIdeas.text: A handful of Marathas against an army.

coreIdeas.text: His kin closed ranks when he fell.

coreIdeas.title: The Eternal Pass
coreIdeas.text: The site of his stand is sacred to Maharashtra.

items.legacy: Bajiprabhu Deshpande is honoured in the ballads and history of Maharashtra as the perfect warrior — the man who gave his life so that his king could live. The pass of Pavan Khind, where he fell, is a place of pilgrimage for every Maratha.

items.name: Netaji Palkar
items.tagline: The first Sarnaubat of the Marathas — the terror of the Mughals
items.attribution: The first commander-in-chief of the Maratha forces
items.quote: The Mughal is a lion at court — but a deer in the field.
items.summary: Netaji Palkar was the first Sarnaubat — commander-in-chief — of the Maratha forces under Shivaji, the fierce warrior who carried the Maratha banners into the Mughal territories and whose raids made the Mughal governors tremble. His life of glory, capture, and return is one of the most dramatic stories of the Maratha age.
overview: A childhood friend and early comrade of Shivaji, Netaji Palkar rose to become the first Sarnaubat, the commander-in-chief of the young Maratha state. He led the Maratha cavalry on the daring campaigns that carried Shivaji's name into the territories of the Mughal empire, raiding and defeating the Mughal detachments that threatened the new kingdom.

His fame grew so great that the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, who had captured Shivaji briefly in 1666, tried to win the commander away from his master: the Mughals captured Palkar and, by a mixture of pressure and temptation, induced him to accept Mughal service and even a nominal conversion — a chapter of his life that the Maratha histories record with sorrow.

According to the tradition, the remorseful Palkar later returned to the Maratha side, repented, and was received back by Shivaji's successors, serving the kingdom again in its wars. His story — of the great commander who fell and rose again — is told as both a warning and a redemption in the Maratha annals.

coreIdeas.text: The first commander-in-chief of the Marathas.

coreIdeas.title: The Raider of the Mughals
coreIdeas.text: His cavalry carried terror to the empire.

coreIdeas.text: The Mughals lured him into service.

coreIdeas.title: The Return
coreIdeas.text: He came back to the Maratha side in the end.

coreIdeas.title: The Dramatic Life
coreIdeas.text: Glory, fall, and redemption in one story.

items.legacy: Netaji Palkar is remembered in Maratha history as the first sword of the new kingdom — the commander who set the pattern of Maratha cavalry warfare. His story is told in Maharashtra as a lesson in glory, temptation, and return.

items.name: General Thimayya
items.tagline: The soldier's general — third Chief of the Army of Bhārat
items.attribution: General K.S. Thimayya — Chief of Army Staff
items.quote: The welfare of the soldier is the first duty of the general.
items.summary: General Kodandera Subayya Thimayya was the third Chief of the Army Staff of independent Bhārat — a soldier of the Kodava country, Karnataka, who served in three wars, earned the love of his troops, and was one of the most admired generals of his time. He later led the UN peacekeeping forces in Cyprus.
overview: Born in Madikeri, Coorg, in 1906, Thimayya was commissioned into the British Indian Army and served with distinction in the Second World War — fighting in Burma against the Japanese, where his leadership earned him the Military Cross. He was one of the officers who emerged of Bhārat from the war as the future leaders of the Army of Bhārat.

After independence, he served with distinction in the wars of 1947-48 and 1962, and rose to become Chief of the Army Staff in 1957. He was known above all as the 'soldier's general' — a commander who shared the hardships of his men, visited the most forward posts, and whose care for the ordinary soldier made him beloved of the entire army.

After retirement he led the United Nations peacekeeping force in Cyprus with great skill, and he died in 1965. His funeral in Coorg, where he was cremated with full military honours, was attended by thousands — a final tribute to the general who had never forgotten the soldier.

coreIdeas.title: The Soldier's General
coreIdeas.text: Famous for his care of the common soldier.

coreIdeas.title: The Third Chief
coreIdeas.text: Chief of Army Staff from 1957.

coreIdeas.title: The Burma Hero

coreIdeas.title: The UN Commander

coreIdeas.title: The Coorg Soldier
coreIdeas.text: Karnataka's greatest military son.

items.legacy: General Thimayya is honoured as one of the most beloved leaders of the Army of Bhārat, and the Madras Regimental Centre at Wellington remembers him with pride. He is the model of the general of Bhārat — brave in war, humane in command.

items.name: Vikramaditya
items.tagline: The emperor of legend — the star of the Vikram Samvat
items.attribution: The legendary emperor of Ujjain
items.quote: The king is the servant of justice — not its master.
items.summary: Vikramaditya is the most famous king of legend of Bhārat — the emperor of Ujjain whose name the Hindu calendar, the Vikram Samvat, bears. In the tradition, he is the just and generous king whose court had the nine gems, or Navaratnas, including the poet Kalidasa, and whose exploits fill the tales of Bhārat.
overview: The name Vikramaditya — 'sun of valour' — is attached in tradition to a great king of Ujjain who drove out the foreign invaders of his age, ruled with justice, and founded an era of such prosperity that his reign was chosen as the starting point of the calendar that bears his name. The Vikram Samvat, which begins in 57 BCE, is still the Hindu and Jain calendar of much of Bhārat.

His court, according to the legend, held the Navaratnas — the nine gems of learning — among them the poet Kalidasa, the lexicographer Amarasimha, and the astronomer Varahamihira, making his reign the model of the golden age of a king who honoured knowledge above gold.

The tales of his justice and generosity fill the storytelling traditions of Bhārat: the cycle of the Vikram and the Vetala, in which the king carries a ghost on his back and answers its riddles, and countless stories of the king who rewarded the good and punished the proud. He remains the archetype of the ideal king of Bhārat — brave, just, and wise.

coreIdeas.title: The Vikram Samvat
coreIdeas.text: The calendar of Bhārat begins with his era.

coreIdeas.title: The Navaratnas
coreIdeas.text: His court held the nine gems of learning.

coreIdeas.title: The Just King
coreIdeas.text: The ideal of justice in every story.

items.legacy: Vikramaditya lives on in the calendar that starts with his era and in the stories told in every language of Bhārat. He is the standard by which tradition measures a king of Bhārat — and the name that every ruler of legend aspires to.

items.name: Onake Obavva
items.tagline: The woman of Chitradurga who slew an army with a pestle
items.attribution: The folk heroine of Chitradurga
items.quote: One woman with a pestle — and a pass to defend — is an army.
items.summary: Onake Obavva was the woman of Chitradurga fort who, alone and armed only with a pestle, defended a narrow pass against the soldiers of Hyder Ali's army in the eighteenth century — killing more than a dozen invaders before she fell. She is honoured as one of the greatest folk heroines of Karnataka.
overview: During the siege of Chitradurga fort by the forces of Hyder Ali in the eighteenth century, the fort's defenders were hard pressed. In the confusion, a small band of the enemy found the secret opening in the rocks — the crevice through which water and grain were carried — and began to enter the fort through the gap.

Obavva, the wife of a guard of the fort, had come to the crevice to fetch water. She saw the soldiers climbing through the opening — and, without raising an alarm that might spread panic, she seized the onake, the long heavy pestle used to pound grain, and took her stand at the crevice. One by one, as each soldier entered the narrow gap, she struck him down — and the pile of the slain grew at the opening.

She killed more than a dozen of the enemy before a soldier struck her from behind in the darkness. Her husband and the fort's garrison, finding the bodies, understood what she had done and sealed the gap. Chitradurga held — and Obavva's stand became the most famous act of bravery in the fort's history.

coreIdeas.text: A grain pestle — her only weapon.

coreIdeas.title: The Crevice

items.legacy: Onake Obavva is honoured with her statue at Chitradurga and her name in the folk songs of Karnataka. She is the proof that courage has no need of armies — a single determined person with a pestle can hold a kingdom's gate.

items.name: Ranjitsinhji
items.tagline: The prince who taught the world to play cricket
items.attribution: K.S. Ranjitsinhji — the 'Ranji' of the Ranji Trophy
items.quote: Cricket is a game of grace — and I play it as I live: with joy.
items.summary: Ranjitsinhji — 'Ranji' — was the first person of Bhārat to play Test cricket and one of the greatest batsmen in the history of the game, the wizard whose leg-glance and late-cut revolutionised batting in Victorian England. The Ranji Trophy, Bhārat's premier domestic cricket championship, bears his name.
overview: Born into the royal family of Nawanagar, Saurashtra, Ranjitsinhji went to England to study at Cambridge — and there the world discovered his genius. In 1896, playing for Sussex, he became the first person of Bhārat in English county cricket, and in 1896–97 he scored over 3,000 runs in a season, the first man ever to do so.

In 1896 he became the first person of Bhārat to play Test cricket, for England — for in his era, Bhārat had no Test team. His batting was pure artistry: the late cut and the leg-glance, strokes no one had ever seen, played with a grace that the great critics called magical. In 1899-1900 he scored 3,000 runs in the season again, and he was voted one of Wisden's Cricketers of the Year.

He returned to Bhārat, ruled his state of Nawanagar as Jam Sahib, and served in the First World War. When cricket needed its own championship of Bhārat in 1934 — the year after his death — the trophy was named the Ranji Trophy in his honour, and his name has crowned every cricketer's ambition ever since.

coreIdeas.title: The 3,000-Run Season

items.legacy: Ranji's name is the highest prize in cricket of Bhārat — the Ranji Trophy that every state team dreams of lifting. He is remembered as the player who proved that a person of Bhārat could be the greatest batsman in the world, a century before the modern era of cricket of Bhārat.

items.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji
items.tagline: The founder of the Maratha empire — the king who defied the Mughals
items.attribution: Shivaji Bhosale — Chhatrapati, founder of the Maratha empire
items.quote: Swarajya is my birthright — and I shall have it.
items.summary: Chhatrapati Shivaji was the greatest king-warrior of Bhārat's medieval age — the founder of the Maratha empire who carved an independent kingdom out of the collapsing empires of the Deccan and defied the might of the Mughals for a lifetime. He built a navy, a fort network, and a state rooted in the soil of Bhārat — and his coronation in 1674 announced a new power in the land.
overview: Born in 1630 in the hill fort of Shivneri, Shivaji grew up under the guidance of his mother Jijabai, who filled him with the tales of the heroes of the epics and the dream of swarajya — self-rule. From his youth he began to seize the forts of the Deccan from the Bijapur sultanate, one by one, building the nucleus of his kingdom.

His life was a series of daring exploits: the escape from the court of Bijapur's ruler in a basket of sweets; the night attack on the Mughal general Shaista Khan in his own camp; the legendary raid on the treasure of Surat; and the escape from Agra, where Aurangzeb had imprisoned him, disguised as a sadhu. His wit was as sharp as his sword.

He was formally crowned Chhatrapati in 1674 with Vedic rites, and built a state remarkable for its justice: a navy that challenged foreign powers, forts that dotted the Sahyadris, and a rule that respected the peasants and the people of every community. He died in 1680, leaving an empire that his successors would carry to the gates of Delhi itself.

coreIdeas.text: 'Self-rule' — the ideal that drove his life and his state.

coreIdeas.title: The Navy

coreIdeas.title: The Coronation of 1674
coreIdeas.text: He founded a kingdom with Vedic rites and a just rule.

items.legacy: Shivaji is the founder of Maratha power and the symbol of the self-assertion of Bhārat against foreign domination. His swarajya inspired the freedom movement, his name is honoured across the land, and his navy, forts, and statesmanship remain a model of Bhārat's own way of war and rule.

items.name: Madakari Nayaka
items.tagline: The last king of Chitradurga — who defied Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan
items.attribution: Madakari Nayaka — the ruler of Chitradurga
items.quote: The fort of Chitradurga has seen many kings — but it has bowed to no master.
items.summary: Madakari Nayaka was the last king of the Paleyagar dynasty of Chitradurga — a ruler of the powerful Nayaka line of the Karnataka country who defied Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan for years. His story, told in the Bharata Bharati series, is the tale of a small kingdom's heroic resistance against the growing power of Mysore.
overview: Chitradurga, the 'fort of the many rocks', was one of the great strongholds of the Karnataka country, ruled by the Nayaka line of chieftains. Madakari Nayaka, born in 1742, inherited a kingdom of forts and hills and a tradition of independence that the rising power of Mysore was determined to crush.

Hyder Ali, the ruler of Mysore, demanded the submission of Chitradurga; Madakari refused, and for years the two powers fought — the hill fort defying the armies of Mysore with a courage that became legend. The people of the region remember him as a just and valiant king who protected his people and his faith against the invader.

In 1779, betrayed from within, the fort fell to Hyder Ali, and Madakari Nayaka was captured and imprisoned. He died in captivity, but the memory of his defiance lived on: the Bharata Bharati series tells his story as one of the great resisters of the South — a king of the people who would not bow.

coreIdeas.text: The great hill stronghold he defended for years.

coreIdeas.title: The Defiance of Mysore

items.legacy: Madakari Nayaka is remembered as one of the great resisters of the South — the last king of Chitradurga who chose defiance over submission. His story is told in the Bharata Bharati series and kept alive in the folk memory of the Karnataka country, a monument to the small kingdoms that fought the great powers of the age.

items.name: Kempegowda
items.tagline: The founder of Bengaluru — the visionary who built the city of the future
items.attribution: Nadaprabhu Kempegowda — the founder of Bengaluru
items.quote: Let a city rise here that will be the talk of the world — a city of lakes, gardens, and justice.
items.summary: Kempegowda was the founder of Bengaluru — the visionary chieftain of the Vokkaliga community who, in 1537, laid the foundation of the city that would become the silicon capital of the world. He built its fort, its lakes, and its temples, and his city grew into one of the greatest of Bhārat.
overview: Born in 1513 into the family of the Morasu Vokkaliga chieftains, Kempegowda succeeded his father as the ruler of the region around Magadi and Yelahanka. A man of great energy and vision, he resolved to build a new capital — and in 1537 he laid the foundation of Bengaluru, named, it is said, after the bende (beans) of the region.

He built the city's fort with a moat, created the great lakes and tanks that still water the city, and raised the temples — including the famous Gavi Gangadhareshwara temple, where the sun's rays touch the idol on Makara Sankranti. He built a city of straight streets and market squares, planned with a vision rare in any age.

He also built a chain of watchtowers around the city — of which the Kempegowda Tower on the city's hill remains — so that no enemy could approach unseen. He died in 1569, but his city grew through the centuries: from the capital of a chieftain to the capital of the state, and today to the technology capital of the world.

items.legacy: Kempegowda is the founder of Bengaluru, one of the great cities of the world — and his vision is visible in every lake and street of the metropolis. His statue and tower stand in the city he built, his name is honoured in its institutions, and his story is the proudest proof that the cities of Bhārat were built by the vision of its own people.

items.name: Mayurasharma
items.tagline: The Brahmin scholar who founded the first Kannada kingdom — the Kadambas
items.attribution: Mayurasharma — the founder of the Kadamba dynasty
items.quote: If they will not give me learning, I will take a kingdom — and learn by ruling it.
items.summary: Mayurasharma was a Brahmin scholar who founded the Kadamba dynasty — the first great kingdom of the Karnataka country, established around 345 CE. According to the famous Talagunda inscription, he took up the sword when a horseman of the Pallavas insulted him, and carved out a kingdom that ruled the west coast for centuries.
overview: The Talagunda inscription, one of the great documents of the history of Karnataka, tells how Mayurasharma — a young Brahmin scholar of the Agrahara at Talagunda — went to Kanchi to complete his vedic studies. There a horseman of the Pallava king insulted and humiliated him, and the scholar's blood rose: he vowed to abandon scholarship and take up the sword.

With the help of the tribes of the forests, he raised an army, defeated the Pallava forces sent against him, and established his kingdom at Banavasi in the forests of the west coast. Thus the first indigenous dynasty of the Kannada country was born — the Kadambas, named, legend says, after the kadamba tree under which the vow was taken.

The Kadamba kingdom grew into a great power, patronising the arts and the religions of the age, and its kings ruled for nearly two hundred years. Mayurasharma's story — the scholar who became a king — is told in the Talagunda inscription as the founding legend of the political history of Karnataka.

items.legacy: Mayurasharma is remembered as the founder of the first great kingdom of Karnataka — the scholar whose pride founded the Kadamba dynasty and began the political history of the Kannada land. His story, preserved in the Talagunda inscription, is the founding legend of the state's identity.

items.name: Ranadhira Kanthirava
items.tagline: The tiger of Mysore — the Wodeyar king who defied the empires
items.attribution: Kanthirava Narasaraja Wodeyar — the ruler of Mysore
items.quote: A lion does not fear the pack — and Mysore does not fear its enemies.
items.summary: Kanthirava Narasaraja Wodeyar, remembered as Ranadhira, 'the heroic in war', was the greatest of the early kings of Mysore — a ruler who expanded his small kingdom, defied the Bijapur sultanate, and made Mysore a power to be reckoned with in the seventeenth century. He was also a patron of music and learning.
overview: Born in 1617, Kanthirava Narasaraja succeeded to the throne of Mysore in 1638, inheriting a small kingdom surrounded by the great powers of the Deccan. He was a born warrior — the account of his reign, the Kanthirava Narasaraja Vijaya, describes his campaigns in detail and records that he personally led his troops in battle after battle.

He expanded Mysore in every direction, taking the forts and towns of the region, and he defeated the armies of the Bijapur sultanate sent to humble him. His kingdom grew into the strongest power of the southern Karnataka country, and his court became a centre of culture — he himself was a musician and a patron of the arts and of learning.

He died in 1659, leaving Mysore enlarged and secure. His grandson's successor Chikkadevaraja would build further on his foundations, but it was Kanthirava who first made Mysore great — the tiger who defied the empires and carved a kingdom by the sword.

coreIdeas.text: He led his armies in person in every campaign.

coreIdeas.title: The Expansion of Mysore
coreIdeas.text: He built the small state into a regional power.

coreIdeas.title: The Defiance of Bijapur

items.legacy: Kanthirava Narasaraja is remembered as the king who first made Mysore great — the warrior who expanded the small kingdom and defied the empires of the age. His name is honoured in the history of the Wodeyar dynasty, and his reign is seen as the foundation on which the later glories of Mysore were built.

items.name: Kumara Rama
items.tagline: The prince of Kampili — the hero of the Kannada folk epics
items.attribution: Kumara Rama — the prince of Kampili
items.quote: A prince of Kampili does not fear death — he fears only dishonour.
items.summary: Kumara Rama was the heroic prince of Kampili — a kingdom of the Karnataka country that defied the Delhi sultanate in the fourteenth century. His story, told in the folk epic Kumara Rama Charite, is one of the great hero-tales of Kannada: a prince of matchless valour who fought the invaders and died for the honour of his land.
overview: Kampili was a small but proud kingdom of the Ballari country, ruled by a line of kings who refused to submit to the sultanate of Delhi as it pushed into the Deccan. Its prince, Kumara Rama, grew up in the traditions of the warrior class, trained in arms and honour from childhood, and became the hero of his people.

The Kumara Rama Charite, one of the great folk epics of Karnataka, tells of his exploits: his battles against the enemies of his kingdom, his loyalty to his father, and his refusal to bow to the invaders. His valour became the talk of the land, and his story was sung across the villages of the Kannada country for centuries.

In the end, the sultanate's forces overwhelmed the small kingdom, and Kumara Rama fell fighting in its defence — a death that made him immortal in the folk memory of Karnataka. His story, preserved in the Bharata Bharati series, remains one of the proudest tales of the resistance of the small kingdoms of the South.

items.legacy: Kumara Rama is one of the great heroes of the folk tradition of Karnataka — the prince who died for the honour of his small kingdom and lives forever in the epics of the land. His story, told in the Bharata Bharati series, keeps alive the memory of the resistance of the small kingdoms of the South.

items.name: Ahilyabai Holkar
items.tagline: The philosopher-queen of Indore — the greatest woman ruler of the Maratha age
items.attribution: Ahilyabai Holkar — the ruler of the Holkar state of Indore
items.quote: The throne is a burden — but the welfare of the people is the reason it is borne.
items.summary: Ahilyabai Holkar was the greatest woman ruler of the Maratha age — the queen of Indore who governed her state for thirty years with a justice and devotion that made her legendary. A devout soul and a brilliant administrator, she is remembered for her temples, her welfare works, and her rule — praised by every historian as a model sovereign.
overview: Born in 1725 in the village of Chondi, Ahilyabai was married into the Holkar family of the Maratha empire. When her father-in-law Malhar Rao Holkar recognised her extraordinary ability, he trained her in the arts of government — and after the deaths of her husband and son, she took the throne of Indore in 1767.

She ruled for thirty years with a rare combination of firmness and compassion. She moved her capital to Maheshwar on the Narmada, administered justice without fear or favour, encouraged trade and agriculture, and built roads and wells and dharmashalas across her state. Her rule was so just that her subjects called her the mother of the land.

She was also one of the great builders of Bhārat: she repaired and built temples from Kashi to Rameswaram, including the renovation of the Kashi Vishwanath temple, and her works still stand across the land. She died in 1795, leaving a state prosperous and a name that has never faded from the memory of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: The Mother of the Land
coreIdeas.text: The title her grateful people gave her.

items.legacy: Ahilyabai Holkar is honoured as the greatest woman ruler of the Maratha age and one of the model sovereigns of Bhārat. Her temples, her welfare works, and her name live on across the land, and every history of Bhārat records her rule as a golden example of justice, devotion, and good governance.

items.name: Banda Bahadur
items.tagline: The Sikh general who avenged the martyrs of the Khalsa
items.attribution: Banda Singh Bahadur — the general of the Khalsa
items.quote: The martyrs of the Khalsa shall be avenged — and the land of the five rivers shall be free.
items.summary: Banda Singh Bahadur was the warrior-saint who led the Sikh rebellion against the Mughal empire after the martyrdom of Guru Gobind Singh. He established the first independent Sikh state in the Punjab, struck at the oppressors of the Khalsa, and faced a martyr's death in Delhi in 1716 — becoming one of the greatest figures of the Sikh tradition.
overview: Born Lachhman Dev in 1670, he was a Bairagi ascetic when he met Guru Gobind Singh in 1708, shortly before the Guru's death. The Guru gave him the name Banda, 'the servant', and charged him with carrying on the struggle of the Khalsa against the Mughal tyranny that had martyred his sons and his followers.

Banda raised the banner of revolt in the Punjab, and within a year he had defeated the Mughal forces, taken Sirhind — the seat of the governors who had martyred the Guru's sons — and established the first independent Sikh state in the land of the five rivers. He struck coins in the name of the Guru, abolished the oppressive levies, and gave the peasants justice.

The Mughal emperor, alarmed, sent a great army against him. After a heroic siege of the fort of Gurdas Nangal, Banda was captured with his followers and taken to Delhi, where he was tortured and executed in 1716 — but his martyrdom kindled the Khalsa's resolve, and his state became the seed of the Sikh sovereignty that would one day rule the Punjab.

coreIdeas.text: Charged by Guru Gobind Singh to continue the struggle.

coreIdeas.title: The First Sikh State
coreIdeas.text: He established independent rule in the Punjab.

coreIdeas.title: Justice for the Peasants
coreIdeas.text: He abolished oppressive levies and gave the people justice.

coreIdeas.title: The Martyr of Delhi
coreIdeas.text: He died for the Khalsa in 1716.

items.legacy: Banda Bahadur is honoured as one of the greatest warriors of the Sikh tradition — the general who established the first Sikh state and avenged the martyrs of the Khalsa. His martyrdom is remembered with reverence, and his name stands beside the Gurus themselves in the history of the Sikh people.

items.name: Mirza Ismail
items.tagline: The great Dewan of Mysore — the architect of its modern glory
items.attribution: Sir Mirza Ismail — the Dewan of Mysore, Jaipur, and Hyderabad
items.quote: A state's greatness is measured not by its palaces but by the welfare of its people.
items.summary: Mirza Ismail was one of the greatest administrators of princely Bhārat — the Dewan of Mysore who, from 1926 to 1941, guided the state to a golden age of industry, education, and public works. Under him Mysore built its great industries, dams, and institutions, and he later served as Dewan of Jaipur and Hyderabad.
overview: Born in Bengaluru in 1883, Mirza Ismail was educated in the state and entered its service young. In 1926 the Maharaja of Mysore appointed him Dewan, and for fifteen years he governed the state with a vision that transformed it into the model of progressive princely rule.

Under his administration Mysore built the great industries — from steel to silk — established the state's electric power, developed irrigation and the Krishna Raja Sagara dam project, and promoted education on a vast scale, including the founding of institutions that made Mysore the most advanced of the princely states. He was the architect of its modern industrial glory.

After Mysore he served as Dewan of Jaipur and of Hyderabad, carrying his administrative genius to those states. He died in 1959, remembered as one of the greatest administrators Bhārat has produced — the man who showed how princely rule could serve the people.

coreIdeas.title: The Great Dewan
coreIdeas.text: Fifteen years of transformative rule in Mysore.

coreIdeas.title: Industry
coreIdeas.text: He built the great industries of the state.

coreIdeas.title: Irrigation and Power
coreIdeas.text: He drove the state's great water and power projects.

coreIdeas.title: Education
coreIdeas.text: He made Mysore a model of learning.

coreIdeas.title: The Model State
coreIdeas.text: Mysore became the most advanced of the princely states.

items.legacy: Mirza Ismail is honoured as one of the greatest administrators in the history of Bhārat — the Dewan who made Mysore the model state of the age. His industries, dams, and institutions still serve the people of Karnataka, and his name remains synonymous with good governance and visionary administration.

items.name: Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar
items.tagline: The Rajarshi of Mysore — the most beloved of its kings
items.attribution: Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV — the Maharaja of Mysore
items.quote: The throne exists for the people — their welfare is the only glory of a king.
items.summary: Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar was the greatest of the Maharajas of Mysore — the 'Rajarshi', the kingly sage, who ruled from 1902 to 1940 and made his state a model of progress for the whole of Bhārat. Under his rule Mysore led the nation in education, industry, and public welfare, and he was loved by his people as few rulers have been.
overview: Born in 1884, Krishnaraja Wodeyar ascended the throne of Mysore in 1902 after a regency. From the start he devoted himself to the welfare of his people, working with great Dewans like Visvesvaraya and Mirza Ismail to make Mysore the most progressive state in Bhārat.

Under his rule Mysore achieved what no other state could: universal education ahead of its time, the great Krishna Raja Sagara dam, the steel works at Bhadravati, the founding of the University of Mysore, and pioneering industries. His government introduced welfare measures, encouraged science and the arts, and made Mysore the envy of the princely states.

He was honoured by his people as Rajarshi, the kingly sage, for his simple life and his devotion to their welfare. He died in 1940, and his people mourned him as a father. His statue stands before the Vidhana Soudha today — the most beloved king of the state of Karnataka.

coreIdeas.title: Rajarshi
coreIdeas.text: 'The kingly sage' — the title his people gave him.

coreIdeas.title: Universal Education
coreIdeas.text: His state led Bhārat in learning.

coreIdeas.title: The KRS Dam
coreIdeas.text: The great dam and industries built under his rule.

coreIdeas.title: The People's King
coreIdeas.text: Loved and mourned as a father by his subjects.

items.legacy: Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar is remembered as the greatest ruler in the history of Mysore and one of the model kings of the world — a ruler who placed the welfare of his people above every glory. His state's institutions still serve Karnataka, and his name is honoured as the Rajarshi who made Mysore great.

items.name: Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar
items.tagline: The builder of Mysore — the king who made it a great power
items.attribution: Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar — the ruler of Mysore
items.quote: A king's duty is to extend his kingdom and enrich his people — both are one work.
items.summary: Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar was the greatest king of Mysore before the age of Hyder Ali — the ruler who, in the late seventeenth century, expanded his small state into the dominant power of the southern Karnataka country. He was also a great builder and administrator who laid the foundations of Mysore's prosperity.
overview: Born in 1673, Chikkadevaraja ascended the throne of Mysore in 1672. He was a brilliant soldier and administrator who, in a reign of more than thirty years, extended his kingdom in every direction, taking the great forts and cities of the region and making Mysore the strongest power of the south of the Karnataka country.

His administration was a model of its age: he organised the revenue system, encouraged trade and agriculture, and built the state's resources with care. He was also a patron of learning — the author himself of works in Kannada — and his court was a centre of culture.

He built the fort and city of Srirangapatna, which his successors would make their capital, and laid the foundations on which the later greatness of Mysore was raised. He died in 1704, remembered as the builder-king who made Mysore a power of the south.

coreIdeas.title: The Expansion
coreIdeas.text: He made Mysore the strongest power of the south.

coreIdeas.title: The Administrator
coreIdeas.text: He reformed revenue and encouraged trade.

coreIdeas.title: The Author King
coreIdeas.text: He wrote works in Kannada himself.

coreIdeas.title: Srirangapatna
coreIdeas.text: He built the future capital of Mysore.

coreIdeas.title: The Builder
coreIdeas.text: His foundations raised the later glory of the state.

items.legacy: Chikkadevaraja Wodeyar is remembered as the builder of Mysore — the king who made the small state a great power and laid the foundations of its prosperity. His name is honoured in the history of the Wodeyar dynasty as the ruler who raised Mysore to greatness.

items.name: Sayajirao Gaekwad
items.tagline: The reformer-Maharaja of Baroda — the model ruler of princely Bhārat
items.attribution: Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda
items.quote: Education is the first duty of a ruler — an uneducated people cannot be a free people.
items.summary: Sayajirao Gaekwad III was the reformer-Maharaja of Baroda — one of the most progressive rulers of princely Bhārat, whose reign of fifty years was a model of good governance. He made primary education compulsory in his state, freed his people from debt, supported the national movement, and patronised learning and the arts without equal.
overview: Born in 1863, Sayajirao was selected to the throne of Baroda in 1875 by the British, who little guessed that they had chosen one of the greatest reformers of the age. Educated and open-minded, he devoted his long reign of more than fifty years to the modernisation of his state.

His achievements were extraordinary: Baroda was the first state in Bhārat to make primary education free and compulsory; he abolished the forced labour of the peasants, freed the state from debt, built universities and institutions, and encouraged industry and agriculture. He supported the cause of the depressed classes and of women's education with funds and favour.

He was a friend of the national movement, supporting leaders like Gandhi and financing the education of the young B.R. Ambedkar. He died in 1939, remembered as the model ruler of princely Bhārat — a king who used his power entirely for the progress of his people.

coreIdeas.title: Compulsory Education
coreIdeas.text: Baroda led Bhārat in universal primary schooling.

coreIdeas.title: The People's Welfare
coreIdeas.text: He freed his peasants from forced labour and debt.

coreIdeas.title: The Friend of Reform
coreIdeas.text: He supported the depressed classes and women's education.

coreIdeas.title: The Patron of Ambedkar
coreIdeas.text: He financed the education of the future constitution-maker.

coreIdeas.title: The Model Ruler
coreIdeas.text: Praised as the best of the princely rulers.

items.legacy: Sayajirao Gaekwad is honoured as the model ruler of princely Bhārat — a king whose fifty-year reign was devoted entirely to the progress of his people. His educational reforms and his patronage changed the lives of millions, and his name remains a standard of enlightened kingship.

items.name: Dewan Purnaiah
items.tagline: The greatest Dewan of Mysore — the architect of its restoration
items.attribution: Purnaiah — the Dewan of Mysore
items.quote: The state is a trust — and the trust must be returned stronger than it was received.
items.summary: Purnaiah was the greatest Dewan of Mysore — the minister who served Tipu Sultan with fidelity, held the state together in its hour of ruin, and then restored the kingdom to the Wodeyar dynasty after the British conquest. His loyalty and administrative genius made him one of the most remarkable statesmen of the age.
overview: Born in 1746, Purnaiah rose through the administration of Mysore to become the trusted minister of Tipu Sultan. When Tipu fell at Srirangapatna in 1799, Purnaiah — with the consent of the British — served as the regent of the young prince, administering Mysore for twelve years with remarkable ability.

His administration restored the prosperity of the war-torn state: he reformed the finances, encouraged agriculture and trade, and rebuilt the kingdom that the wars had ruined. His justice and efficiency won the respect even of the British, who called him one of the ablest ministers of the age.

He retired in 1811, having handed the state back to the Wodeyar king in good order, and died in 1812. He is remembered as the model of the loyal minister — a statesman who served his state through its greatest crisis and left it stronger than he found it.

coreIdeas.title: The Minister of Tipu
coreIdeas.text: He served the Sultan with total fidelity.

coreIdeas.title: The Regent
coreIdeas.text: He governed Mysore for twelve years after 1799.

coreIdeas.title: The Restorer
coreIdeas.text: He rebuilt the war-torn state's prosperity.

coreIdeas.title: The Just Administrator
coreIdeas.text: Respected even by the British for his ability.

coreIdeas.title: The Loyal Servant
coreIdeas.text: He handed the state back in good order.

items.legacy: Dewan Purnaiah is remembered as one of the greatest statesmen of the age — the minister who held Mysore together through its ruin and restored it to prosperity. His name is honoured in the history of Karnataka as the model of the able and loyal administrator.

items.name: Field Marshal K.M. Cariappa
items.tagline: The first Commander-in-Chief of the Indian Army
items.attribution: Kodandera Madappa Cariappa — the first Indian Commander-in-Chief
items.quote: I am an Indian first and an officer after — my loyalty is to the flag of the republic.
items.summary: Field Marshal K.M. Cariappa was the first Indian to command the Indian Army — the soldier from a small town of Karnataka who rose to the highest rank of the forces and took command of the army of independent Bhārat in 1949. He served in two world wars, led the nation's forces with distinction, and was honoured with the rank of Field Marshal in 1986.
overview: Born in 1899 in Shanivarsanthe in the Kodagu country of Karnataka, Cariappa joined the army young and served in the First World War in Mesopotamia. Between the wars he rose steadily, serving in the army of the empire, and in the Second World War he commanded troops in the Burma campaign with distinction.

When Bhārat became independent in 1947, the new nation faced its first test in the war in Kashmir — and Cariappa, as a senior general, helped direct the defence of the new state. In January 1949 he became the first Indian Commander-in-Chief of the Indian Army, succeeding the last British commander.

He served as the army's head till 1953, and after retirement continued to serve the nation in various capacities. In 1986 the nation honoured him with the rank of Field Marshal — only the second in its history — and he died in 1993 at the age of ninety-three, the father of the Indian Army.

coreIdeas.title: The First Indian Commander
coreIdeas.text: The first Indian to command the Indian Army.

coreIdeas.title: The World Wars
coreIdeas.text: He served in Mesopotamia and Burma.

coreIdeas.title: The Kashmir War
coreIdeas.text: He helped direct the defence of the new nation.

coreIdeas.title: Field Marshal

coreIdeas.title: The Soldier's Patriot
coreIdeas.text: His loyalty to the republic was absolute.

items.legacy: Field Marshal K.M. Cariappa is honoured as the father of the Indian Army — the soldier who carried the command of the nation's forces from the empire to the republic. His name is given to the army's institutions and honours, and his life remains the model of the soldier's duty and the patriot's love.

items.name: Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw
items.tagline: Sam Bahadur — the architect of Bhārat's greatest military victory
items.attribution: Sam Hormusji Framji Jamshedji Manekshaw — the Chief of Army Staff
items.quote: In war, as in peace, the soldier's duty is clear: serve the nation, whatever it costs.
items.summary: Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw, Sam Bahadur to his men, was the greatest soldier of independent Bhārat — the Chief of Army Staff who planned and led the 1971 war that freed Bangladesh and broke Pakistan in two. He served in five wars across a career of four decades and was honoured with the rank of Field Marshal, the first Indian to receive it.
overview: Born in 1914 in Amritsar to a Parsi family, Manekshaw joined the Indian Military Academy in its first batch and was commissioned in 1934. In the Second World War he was gravely wounded in Burma, and — in a famous moment — was awarded the Military Cross after insisting on rejoining the battle.

He served the new nation in the wars of 1947, 1962, and 1965, rising to become the Chief of Army Staff in 1969. When the crisis over East Pakistan came in 1971, Manekshaw — against the impatience of politicians — insisted on the right timing and the full preparation, and then executed a campaign of genius that led to the surrender of ninety thousand Pakistani soldiers and the birth of Bangladesh.

For that victory he was honoured with the Padma Vibhushan and, in 1973, the rank of Field Marshal — the first Indian to hold it. He died in 2008, remembered as Sam Bahadur, the most loved and respected soldier of the nation.

coreIdeas.title: The 1971 War
coreIdeas.text: The campaign that freed Bangladesh and broke Pakistan.

coreIdeas.title: The First Field Marshal
coreIdeas.text: The first Indian honoured with the highest rank.

coreIdeas.title: Five Wars
coreIdeas.text: He served in every war of his generation.

coreIdeas.title: The Burma Wound
coreIdeas.text: He won the Military Cross in the Second World War.

coreIdeas.title: Sam Bahadur
coreIdeas.text: The name his men gave the greatest of their chiefs.

items.legacy: Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw is honoured as the greatest soldier of independent Bhārat — the architect of its greatest military victory and the first Indian Field Marshal. His name is given to the army's honours and institutions, and his courage, wit, and loyalty remain the model of the Indian soldier.

items.name: Aryabhata
items.tagline: The astronomer who declared that the earth moves
items.attribution: The first great astronomer and mathematician of Bhārat
items.quote: The earth is a sphere that spins on its own axis — and the stars are fixed.
items.summary: Aryabhata was the first great astronomer and mathematician of Bhārat — the scientist who, in the fifth century, declared that the earth rotates on its axis, explained the causes of eclipses correctly, and computed the value of pi with remarkable accuracy. Bhārat's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named in his honour.
overview: Born in 476 CE, Aryabhata worked at Pataliputra, the great city of the Gupta age, and there he wrote the Aryabhatiya, a masterwork that gathered astronomy and mathematics into one brilliant book. He was barely twenty-three when he composed it, and the book set the standard for science for centuries of Bhārat.

His astronomy was breathtakingly ahead of its time: he declared that the earth rotates on its axis daily, that the moon shines by reflected sunlight, and that eclipses are caused by the shadow of the earth falling on the moon — and vice versa — not by demons swallowing the luminaries, as the popular belief held. He calculated the length of the year with stunning precision and explained that the apparent motion of the stars was due to the earth's own motion.

In mathematics he gave the value of pi as 3.1416, worked with the place-value system and its zeros, and wrote on the solution of equations — the sine table he produced is among the earliest in the world. His methods were carried to the Arab world and Europe, and his name travelled with them. Modern Bhārat honours him with the Aryabhata satellite and the nation's highest award in mathematics.

coreIdeas.title: The Moving Earth
coreIdeas.text: He declared the earth rotates on its axis, 1,000 years before Copernicus.

coreIdeas.title: The True Eclipse

coreIdeas.title: The Value of Pi

items.legacy: Aryabhata is honoured as the father of astronomy and mathematics of Bhārat, and his work is taught in every school of the nation. His insight that the earth moves — a millennium before Europe — is the proof of Bhārat's ancient scientific genius.

items.name: J.C. Bose
items.tagline: The scientist who proved that plants feel
items.attribution: Sir Jagadish Chandra Bose — physicist and plant physiologist
items.quote: The boundary between the living and the non-living is thinner than we think.
items.summary: Jagadish Chandra Bose was the Bengali polymath who proved that plants have life and feeling — inventing the crescograph, a device so sensitive it recorded a plant's pulse. He was also a pioneer of radio waves and of science fiction, and the founder of the Bose Institute, the first great research institute of modern Bhārat.
overview: Bose was a brilliant student who took the Natural Sciences Tripos at Cambridge after studying at Calcutta. He was appointed professor of physics at Presidency College, Calcutta, where — refused proper apparatus by the British administration — he built his own instruments with scrap metal, a habit of self-reliance that defined his science.

His research on the newly discovered radio waves, carried out in the 1890s, predated and paralleled Marconi's work — he demonstrated the wireless transmission of signals in Calcutta in 1895, a year before Marconi's patent. He is honoured as a pioneer of wireless communication.

His most famous work was on plant life: he invented the crescograph, which magnified the movements of plants thousands of times, and proved that plants respond to touch, drugs, and injury with the same electrical signals as animals. His book 'Response in the Living and Non-Living' is a classic. He founded the Bose Institute in 1917, and he died in 1937, honoured as one of the founders of modern science of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.text: His instrument recorded the pulse of plants.

coreIdeas.title: The Plant's Feeling
coreIdeas.text: He proved plants respond to touch and harm.

coreIdeas.title: The Radio Pioneer
