items.legacy: Every film of Bhārat, from the first silent to the latest blockbuster, descends from Phalke's 1913 gamble. His name crowns the Phalke Award, the dream of every filmmaker, and his story — the man who sold his insurance to build a screen for Bhārat — is the founding legend of the world's largest film industry.

items.name: Raja Ravi Varma
items.tagline: The painter who gave Bhārat its gods — the first master of the modern canvas of Bhārat
items.attribution: Ravi Varma — the painter-prince of Travancore
items.quote: The gods of Bhārat are real to me — I paint them as I see them.
items.quoteSource: The spirit of Raja Ravi Varma
items.summary: Raja Ravi Varma was the first painter to master of Bhārat modern oil painting — and the first to bring the gods of Bhārat to the common home. His images of Lakshmi, Saraswati, and the heroes of the epics, printed by the lakh in his own press, shaped how Bhārat imagines its divinities to this day.
overview: Born in the princely state of Travancore in 1848, Ravi Varma showed an astonishing gift for drawing as a child, and the royal house gave him the training of European masters — oil, light, and perspective, taught against the backdrop of Kerala's temples and its rich traditional art.

He painted the royal families of Bhārat, but his heart was in the epics: his scenes of Shakuntala, Damayanti, and the battles and sorrows of the Ramayana and Mahabharata astonished Bhārat, for he painted the gods as living men and women, with skin, light, and tears. His genius won him the title of Raja from the British, and the Kaiser-e-Hind, but his greatest prize was the home of Bhārat.

In 1894 he established a lithographic press in Bombay so that his paintings could be printed cheaply — and millions of prints of Lakshmi, Saraswati, Krishna, and Ganesha flooded the country. That imagery became the visual language of devotion of Bhārat, the basis of calendar art, and the face of the gods in every shrine. He died in 1906, leaving a style that still defines how Bhārat sees its mythology.

coreIdeas.title: The Modern Master
coreIdeas.text: The first person of Bhārat to master oil painting.

coreIdeas.title: The Gods as People

items.legacy: Ravi Varma's Lakshmi and Saraswati still smile from the walls of millions of homes of Bhārat, and his style shaped calendar art, cinema posters, and the very idea of the divine in modern Bhārat. He is honoured as the father of modern art of Bhārat — the painter who gave the nation its gods.

items.name: Nandalal Bose
items.tagline: The painter of the national spirit — the master of Santiniketan
items.attribution: Nandalal Bose — the greatest pupil of Abanindranath Tagore
items.quote: Art is the soul's answer to the world — Bhārat must paint with Bhārat's own brush.
items.summary: Nandalal Bose was the greatest painter of modern Bhārat after Ravi Varma — the master of Santiniketan who gave the art revival of Bhārat its deepest roots in folk, Ajanta, and village tradition. He painted Bhārat's history, Bhārat's people, and Bhārat's soul, and his work is the bridge between the classical past and the modern nation.
overview: Born in 1882, Nandalal Bose came to Calcutta at the height of the Bengal renaissance and joined the school of Abanindranath Tagore, the founder of the new painting of Bhārat. But where his master looked to the Mughal and Rajput miniatures, Nandalal reached deeper — to Ajanta, to folk art, to the village crafts of the land.

In 1922 he joined Tagore's Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan and there built the great Kala Bhavan, the art school that became the heart of modern art of Bhārat. He painted the great murals of history — the lives of the Buddha and of the freedom movement — and his students, the first generation of independent Bhārat's artists, carried his vision across the country.

His greatest honour came with independence: in 1930, Gandhi himself invited him to create the art for the Congress sessions, and his sketches of Gandhi and of Bhārat's villagers became the visual record of the freedom struggle. He died in 1966, honoured as the father of the national school of painting, and the government of Bhārat later issued his paintings on its stamps — the mark of a national master.

coreIdeas.title: The Kala Bhavan
coreIdeas.text: He built Santiniketan's great school of art.

coreIdeas.title: The Folk Soul
coreIdeas.text: He rooted art in village of Bhārat and Ajanta tradition.

coreIdeas.title: The Gandhi Sketches
coreIdeas.text: His drawings captured the freedom movement.

coreIdeas.title: The National Master
coreIdeas.text: His murals painted Bhārat's history.

coreIdeas.title: The Teacher of Masters
coreIdeas.text: He trained the first generation of independent Bhārat.

items.legacy: Nandalal Bose is honoured as the father of the modern school of painting of Bhārat. His images of Gandhi and of Bhārat's villages are part of the national memory, and the Kala Bhavan he built still trains the painters of Bhārat — the living school of the nation's art.

items.name: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan
items.tagline: The Tansen of the twentieth century — the voice of the Patiala gharana
items.attribution: Ustad Bade Ghulam Ali Khan — the supreme vocalist of his age
items.quote: Sing so that the stone of the heart melts — that is the purpose of the raga.
items.summary: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan was the greatest Hindustani vocalist of the twentieth century — the supreme master of the Patiala gharana, whose voice could move from the deepest bass to the highest note in a single breath. Called the Tansen of his age, he made the khyal and the thumri soar to a level no singer of his time approached.
overview: Born in 1902 in Kasur, in the musical family that founded the Patiala gharana, Bade Ghulam Ali Khan grew up singing the traditional forms — the khyal, the thumri, the dadra — and was trained by his father and his uncle, Ali Baksh, in the rigorous disciplines of the gharana. His voice, deep and powerful from boyhood, was shaped into the most flexible instrument of his generation.

His fame crossed Bhārat in the 1930s and 1940s: his concerts drew crowds that filled stadiums, and his recordings sold as no classical singer's had before. His mastery of the thumri, the romantic song of the North, and his electrifying tans — the rapid runs of notes — made him the model of the modern khayal singer, and every great vocalist since has studied his art.

After the partition of 1947 he moved to Bhārat, settling in Bombay and Lahore's loss becoming Bhārat's gain. His voice — heard in films like Mughal-e-Azam's divine opening — carried the classical tradition to the common listener. He died in 1968, and his singing, praised by every critic as the highest point of the age, remains the standard against which Hindustani vocalism is measured.

coreIdeas.title: The Patiala Gharana
coreIdeas.text: The supreme master of Punjab's great singing school.

coreIdeas.title: The Thumri
coreIdeas.text: He made the romantic song of the North a high art.

coreIdeas.title: The Tans
coreIdeas.text: His lightning runs of notes are the legend of the khayal.

coreIdeas.title: The Mughal-e-Azam Voice
coreIdeas.text: His singing crowned Bhārat's greatest film.

coreIdeas.title: The Tansen of the Age
coreIdeas.text: The title given him by critics and kings alike.

items.legacy: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan's recordings are the textbooks of every classical singer of North Bhārat, and his thumris still move audiences to tears. He is honoured as the voice that carried the raga from the courts to the concert hall — the Tansen of the twentieth century.

items.name: Bala Gandharva
items.tagline: The greatest singer-actor of Marathi theatre — the nightingale of the stage
items.attribution: Narayan Shripad Rajhans — 'Bala Gandharva'
items.quote: The stage is a temple — and the actor must enter it as a priest.
items.summary: Bala Gandharva was the greatest figure of the Marathi stage — a singer and actor whose voice and grace made him the most beloved performer of his age, and whose female roles — in the era before actresses — were so perfect that audiences wept. His songs became the household music of Maharashtra, and his name remains the highest honour of the Marathi theatre.
overview: Born Narayan Rajhans in 1888, he joined a theatre company as a boy and was given the name Bala Gandharva — 'the divine singer of the stage' — for the beauty of his voice. In an age when respectable women did not act, the young Bala Gandharva played the heroines, and his performances of Manini and of the great female roles of Marathi drama made him the darling of the Marathi home.

His art was double: his singing, of the light classical forms that the theatre used, was sweet enough to draw crowds for the music alone, and his acting, of love, grief, and devotion, was so moving that the audiences of Bombay and Poona treated him with the reverence due to a temple singer. His name is the bridge between the classical music of Maharashtra and its popular stage.

He acted and sang for more than forty years, making his last appearance in the 1950s, and died in 1967. Maharashtra gave him a funeral worthy of a prince, and the Balgandharva Rangmandir — the theatre named after him — stands in Pune as his monument, while his gramophone records still sell and his songs still play in Marathi homes.

coreIdeas.title: The Divine Singer
coreIdeas.text: His voice made him the nightingale of the Marathi stage.

coreIdeas.title: The Female Roles
coreIdeas.text: He played the heroines of the age with perfect grace.

coreIdeas.title: The Stage as Temple
coreIdeas.text: He raised Marathi theatre to devotion.

coreIdeas.title: The Records
coreIdeas.text: His songs became the household music of Maharashtra.

coreIdeas.title: The Rangmandir
coreIdeas.text: Pune's great theatre bears his name.

items.legacy: Bala Gandharva is honoured as the crown of the Marathi stage and one of the greatest singer-actors Bhārat has produced. His records still play, his theatre still stands, and his name is the highest title of honour a Marathi performer can receive.

items.name: Bidaram Krishnappa
items.tagline: The court singer of Mysore — the voice that crowned the great dynasty's music
items.attribution: Bidaram Krishnappa — the asthana vidwan of Mysore
items.quote: The song is the soul of the tradition — sing the master's word as the master sang it.
items.summary: Bidaram Krishnappa was one of the greatest Carnatic vocalists of the Mysore court — the asthana vidwan whose singing of the great composers' kritis, and whose mastery of the music of Tyagaraja and the Mysore tradition, made him the standard of the age. His name is the bridge between the royal patronage of Mysore and the concert music of today.
overview: Born in Mysore in 1866, Bidaram Krishnappa grew up in the richest musical atmosphere of South Bhārat — the court of the Wodeyar maharajas, which gathered the greatest musicians of the age and patronized the music of Tyagaraja and his tradition with royal generosity.

He rose to become the asthana vidwan, the court singer, of Mysore — a position of the highest honour — and his concerts, his disciples, and his recordings carried the Mysore style of Carnatic music across the south. His singing of the kritis, with the precise diction and the deep bhava of the tradition, was the model for a generation of musicians.

He also served the tradition as a teacher, training some of the finest vocalists of the next generation, and as a composer and scholar of the Mysore style. He died in 1931, leaving the Mysore court's music in the safekeeping of his disciples — and his name still honours the annual festival of music that Mysore holds in memory of its great singers.

coreIdeas.text: The asthana vidwan of the great Mysore court.

coreIdeas.title: The Kriti Master

coreIdeas.title: The Mysore Style

items.legacy: Bidaram Krishnappa is honoured as one of the pillars of the Mysore musical tradition, and his name lives in the concerts and the festival of the city he sang for. He is remembered as the proof that the royal courts of Bhārat were the nurseries of its greatest music.

items.name: Veene Sheshanna
items.tagline: The prince of the veena — the divine instrument made to speak
items.attribution: Sheshanna — the asthana vidwan of Mysore
items.quote: The veena is the voice of the goddess — the musician only lends it his hands.
items.summary: Veene Sheshanna was the greatest veena player Bhārat has produced — the court musician of Mysore whose mastery of the sacred instrument earned him the title of 'Tansen of the veena' and whose concerts were the wonder of South Bhārat. He made the veena sing as a voice, and his name remains the highest honour of the instrument.
overview: Born in Mysore in 1852 into a family of court musicians, Sheshanna was trained in the veena from childhood and became a prodigy of the instrument. The Maharaja of Mysore, recognizing his genius, made him the asthana vidwan of the court — and his concerts, at the court and across South Bhārat, drew the same wonder as the greatest singers'.

His playing was famous for its vocal quality — he made the veena sing the raga with the sweetness of a voice, and his mastery of the gamaka, the ornamentation of Carnatic music, was unmatched. Musicians said that to hear Sheshanna was to hear the goddess Saraswati herself, and the Maharaja honoured him with the title of 'the Tansen of the veena'.

He trained a school of disciples and raised the veena to a place of honour in the concerts of the south. He died in 1926, and his name passed into the tradition: the Veene Sheshanna style, the Veene Sheshanna tradition, still taught and played by the instrument's masters, is his living monument.

coreIdeas.title: The Instrument's King
coreIdeas.text: The greatest veena player of Bhārat.

coreIdeas.title: The Tansen of the Veena
coreIdeas.text: The title the Maharaja of Mysore gave him.

coreIdeas.title: The Vocal Veena
coreIdeas.text: He made the instrument sing like a voice.

coreIdeas.title: The Gamaka Master

coreIdeas.title: The Living Style
coreIdeas.text: His tradition is still taught to veena masters.

items.legacy: Veene Sheshanna's name is the highest honour of the veena — the Veene Sheshanna tradition is still the standard of the instrument, and his concerts are the golden legend of Mysore's music. He is remembered as the proof that the sacred instrument of Bhārat can speak with the sweetness of the human voice.

items.name: Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande
items.tagline: The father of modern Hindustani musicology
items.attribution: Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande — the systematiser of Hindustani music
items.quote: The ragas of Bhārat are a science — and a science must be taught systematically.
items.summary: Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande was the father of modern Hindustani musicology — the scholar who travelled the length of Bhārat collecting the great compositions of the past, and who organised the vast field of Hindustani music into the system of ragas and thaats that is taught in every school today. His work saved the classical music of the North from chaos and decline.
overview: Born in 1860 in a family of musicians and scholars, Bhatkhande was a lawyer by profession and a musician by passion. He devoted his life to the study of the music of the North, and in the course of his research he travelled across Bhārat, meeting the great ustads and gathering their compositions before the tradition was lost.

His greatest achievement was the systematisation of Hindustani music: he classified the ragas into ten thaats, or scale-types, a system that became the foundation of music education. He wrote the great four-volume Hindustani Sangeet Paddhati, the standard textbook of the art, and his notation system made it possible to write down and preserve the compositions of the masters.

He founded the music colleges at Lucknow, Gwalior, and Baroda, and died in 1936, honoured as the father of modern musicology in the North. His system is still the basis of every music school of Hindustani music.

items.legacy: Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande is honoured as the father of modern Hindustani musicology — the scholar whose system of ragas and notation is the foundation of every music school of the North. His collections and textbooks saved the tradition, and his name remains the greatest in the modern study of Hindustani music.

items.name: Vishnu Digambar Paluskar
items.tagline: The apostle of music for the people — the founder of the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya
items.attribution: Vishnu Digambar Paluskar — the singer and music educator
items.quote: Music belongs to the people — let it leave the courts and enter every home.
items.summary: Vishnu Digambar Paluskar was one of the greatest figures in the history of Hindustani music — the singer who carried the classical art from the courts and private houses into the public concert and the school. He founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya, the first great public music school of the North, and used music in the service of the nation.
overview: Born in 1872, Paluskar was a blind singer of extraordinary gifts — he lost his sight as a child but developed a voice that moved all who heard it. He trained under the great masters of the Gwalior tradition, and he resolved to do what no musician had done: to take music from the closed circles of the rich into the public domain.

In 1901 he founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in Lahore, the first music school open to all, where music was taught systematically and publicly. The institution, which spread to other cities, trained a generation of musicians and made music education accessible to everyone — breaking the monopoly of the hereditary masters.

He was also a patriot: he sang at the Congress sessions, used his art for the nation, and his public concerts made classical music a national possession. He died in 1931, honoured as the apostle of music for the people, and the modern public concert owes its existence to his vision.

items.legacy: Vishnu Digambar Paluskar is honoured as the apostle of music for the people — the singer who carried Hindustani music from the courts into every home and school. His Gandharva Mahavidyalaya trained the musicians of the modern age, and his vision of music as the possession of the nation is the foundation of the public concert today.

items.name: Veene Subbanna
items.tagline: The prince of the veena — the golden voice of Mysore's music
items.attribution: Subbanna — the veena player and singer of Mysore
items.quote: The veena is the goddess's instrument — let it speak the raga as the voice speaks the song.
items.summary: Veene Subbanna was one of the great jewels of the music of Mysore — a musician of the royal court whose veena playing and singing made him one of the most honoured artists of the age. He lived a life of ease and pleasure, yet was a man of extraordinary generosity, giving away lakhs in charity and honouring learning and talent without jealousy.
overview: Born in 1861 in Mysore, Subbanna grew up in the richest musical atmosphere of the South — the court of the Wodeyar maharajas, which gathered the greatest musicians of the age. He became a master of the veena and of vocal music, and his performances were counted among the wonders of the state.

The account of his life in the Bharata Bharati series records that to hear him play the veena was a blessing — his music drew the rasikas, the connoisseurs, of the whole South. He lived a life of enjoyment, as the fortunate of his age did, but his heart was generous: he gave lakhs of rupees in charity and honoured the learning of others without a trace of jealousy.

He died in 1939, honoured as one of the great musicians of Mysore. His name is remembered in the musical tradition of the state, and his life is remembered for the union of great art with great generosity.

items.legacy: Veene Subbanna is remembered as one of the great musicians of the Mysore court — an artist whose veena playing was a wonder of the age and whose generosity was as great as his art. His name is honoured in the musical tradition of Karnataka, and his life is remembered as the union of art and largesse.

items.name: Panchakshari Gavai
items.tagline: The saint-singer of the North Karnataka — the voice of devotion
items.attribution: Panchakshari Gavai — the singer of the Dharwad tradition
items.quote: The raga and the devotion are one — sing so that the heart of the listener turns to God.
items.summary: Panchakshari Gavai was one of the greatest singers of the Dharwad tradition of North Karnataka — a master of the Hindustani khayal whose concerts were the wonder of the age. A singer of matchless depth and devotion, he carried the great ragas of the North to the concert halls of the South and trained a generation of musicians.
overview: Born in 1898 in Dharwad, Panchakshari Gavai grew up in one of the great musical centres of the South, and his voice was recognised as extraordinary from his youth. He trained in the Hindustani tradition, mastering the khayal and the great ragas with a depth that few of his contemporaries could match.

His concerts, in the major cities of the South and across the country, were events of the highest order — his singing of the great ragas moved audiences to a state of absorption that was almost devotional. He was among the singers who carried the Hindustani tradition of the Dharwad region to national fame.
He was also a devoted teacher, training a generation of musicians in the tradition. He died in 1953, honoured as one of the greatest voices of the age — a singer whose art was a form of worship.

His name is remembered in the musical life of Karnataka, and his art remains the standard of the devotional depth of the raga.

items.name: Vasudevacharya
items.tagline: The composer-saint of Mysore — the jewel of Carnatic music
items.attribution: Mysore Vasudevacharya — the composer and singer
items.quote: The kriti is the prayer of the South — and the composer is its priest.
items.summary: Mysore Vasudevacharya was one of the greatest composers and singers of Carnatic music — the court musician of Mysore who lived for nearly a century and whose kritis, in Sanskrit and Kannada, are among the treasures of the tradition. His life spanned the golden age of Mysore's music, and his compositions are sung in every concert of the South.
overview: Born in 1865 in Mysore, Vasudevacharya was a child prodigy of music — he began composing at the age of nine and was recognised by the greatest musicians of the age. He became the asthana vidwan, the court musician, of Mysore, serving the Wodeyar court for decades.

He was a prolific composer: his kritis, set in the classical ragas, are sung in concerts across the South, and his command of Sanskrit and Kannada made his lyrics works of literature as well as music. He was also a great singer and teacher, and his students carried his tradition across the land.

He lived to the age of ninety-six, dying in 1961 — a life that spanned from the age of the great composers to the modern concert. He is honoured as the last of the great composer-saints of the Carnatic tradition, and his kritis remain the treasure of the music of the South.

His century-long life spanned the golden age of the music, and his compositions remain the treasure of the tradition.

items.name: Bellary Raghava
items.tagline: The prince of the Kannada stage — the greatest actor of his age
items.attribution: Bellary Raghava — the actor of the Kannada stage
items.quote: The actor must become the character — the stage is the temple of the soul's truth.
items.summary: Bellary Raghava was the greatest actor of the Kannada stage — a performer whose genius made him the most celebrated figure of the theatre of Karnataka and of the Tamil stage as well. His acting, in the great mythological and historical plays of the age, drew audiences that filled the theatres, and his name became the very word for great acting in the South.
overview: Born in 1880 in Bellary, Raghava was drawn to the theatre in his youth and joined the drama companies of the age, rising rapidly by his extraordinary talent. He became the leading actor of the Kannada and Tamil stages, playing the great roles — from mythological heroes to historical figures — with a power that held audiences spellbound.

His acting was famous for its intensity and its truth: he studied each character so deeply that he seemed to become it, and his performances in the classic plays of the repertoire are still remembered as the highest points of the stage of the age. His fame spread beyond Karnataka to the Tamil country, where he was equally adored.

He was also a reformer of the theatre, working to raise its standards, and a generous man who gave freely. He died in 1946, honoured as the prince of the Kannada stage — the greatest actor his people had produced.

items.legacy: Bellary Raghava is honoured as the prince of the Kannada stage — the greatest actor of his age, whose performances are still remembered as the highest points of the theatre of the South. His name remains the standard of great acting in Karnataka, and his art is part of the golden history of the stage.

items.name: Madurai Mani Iyer
items.tagline: The voice of the South — the master of the Carnatic concert
items.attribution: Madurai Mani Iyer — the Carnatic vocalist
items.quote: Sing with the joy of the heart — the raga must dance, not merely sound.
items.summary: Madurai Mani Iyer was one of the greatest Carnatic vocalists of the modern age — a singer whose voice, brimming with joy and energy, made him the most loved musician of the South in his time. His concerts, famous for their brilliance and their sparkling style, remain the model of the Carnatic concert for every singer.
overview: Born in 1912 in Madurai, Mani Iyer was a prodigy of music who rose to fame in his youth. His voice, his speed, and his joy in singing made his concerts events of extraordinary excitement, and he became one of the most popular musicians of the South — his concerts drawing crowds wherever he performed.

His style was the delight of the connoisseurs: the sparkling briga runs, the brilliant swaras, and the sheer joy of the music made every concert a celebration. He was also a master of the kriti, singing the great compositions of the tradition with feeling and precision.

He died in 1968, at the height of his fame, and the South mourned the loss of its most loved voice. His recordings remain the treasure of the tradition, and his name is remembered as the master of the joyful Carnatic concert.

items.name: Pannalal Ghosh
items.tagline: The master of the flute — who raised the bansuri to the concert stage
items.attribution: Pannalal Ghosh — the flautist
items.quote: The flute is the voice of the divine — let it speak the deepest ragas of the North.
items.summary: Pannalal Ghosh was the master of the flute of Hindustani music — the musician who transformed the humble bansuri into a full concert instrument capable of the deepest ragas of the North. His playing, at once powerful and tender, made the flute a first-rank instrument of the classical stage.
overview: Born in 1911 in Barisal, Pannalal Ghosh was drawn to the flute from childhood and trained under the great masters of the Hindustani tradition. He realised that the small folk flute could not express the full range of the classical raga, and he redesigned it — creating the larger, deeper bansuri that could carry the music of the concert stage.

His mastery of the instrument was revolutionary: he played the full range of the khayal tradition on the flute, performing the great ragas with a depth and power that no one had thought the instrument capable of. His concerts established the flute as a first-rank instrument of Hindustani music.
He died in 1960, at the height of his powers. He is honoured as the father of the modern concert flute of the North — the master who gave the instrument its voice and its place on the great stage.

items.legacy: Pannalal Ghosh is honoured as the father of the modern concert flute — the master who raised the bansuri from a folk instrument to the great stage of Hindustani music. His redesigned instrument and his playing transformed the tradition, and his name is remembered wherever the flute of the North is heard.

items.name: Muthiah Bhagavathar
items.tagline: The composer and singer of the Harikatha — the pride of Thanjavur
items.attribution: Harikesanallur Muthiah Bhagavathar — the musician and composer
items.quote: The song must carry the story — and the story must carry the soul to God.
items.summary: Muthiah Bhagavathar was one of the greatest musicians and composers of the Carnatic tradition — a master of the Harikatha, the musical narration of the sacred stories, and a composer of more than four hundred kritis. He was honoured with the title of Gayaka Sikhamani, 'the crest-jewel of singers', and his compositions remain the treasure of the South.
overview: Born in 1877 in Harikesanallur, Muthiah Bhagavathar was trained in music and Sanskrit from childhood and became a master of both. He served as the court musician of the Maharaja of Travancore and later of Mysore, and his Harikatha performances — the musical telling of the epics and the puranas — were famous across the South.

He composed more than four hundred kritis, in Sanskrit, Tamil, and Telugu, and his compositions — set in the classical ragas — are sung in concerts to this day. He also created new ragas and enriched the theory of the music of the South.

He died in 1945, honoured as the Gayaka Sikhamani, the crest-jewel of singers. His compositions remain the treasure of the Carnatic tradition, and his name is remembered as one of the greatest musician-composers of the South.

items.legacy: Muthiah Bhagavathar is honoured as one of the greatest musicians and composers of the Carnatic tradition — the Gayaka Sikhamani whose kritis are sung in every concert of the South. His compositions remain the treasure of the tradition, and his name is remembered as the pride of Thanjavur and of Carnatic music.

items.name: Basavappa Shastri
items.tagline: The father of Kannada theatre — the maker of the modern stage
items.attribution: Basavappa Shastri — the pioneer of the Kannada stage
items.quote: The stage of the people must speak the language of the people — and the tales of the land.
items.summary: Basavappa Shastri was the father of Kannada theatre — the scholar and poet who brought the modern stage to the Kannada land and wrote the plays that founded its dramatic literature. His extraordinary learning, his poetic gifts, and his sweet voice made him the maker of the Kannada theatre of Mysore.
overview: Born in 1843, Basavappa Shastri was a scholar of astonishing learning — a master of Sanskrit and Kannada, a poet of genius, and a musician of a sweet voice. He served in the court of Mysore, where his talents won him honour, and he was drawn to the new art of the theatre that was spreading across Bhārat.

He translated the great Sanskrit plays into Kannada and wrote original dramas, founding the dramatic literature of the language. The account of his life in the Bharata Bharati series records that his Kaya Srigowri and his other plays were beloved by the people of Mysore, and his productions were the beginning of the modern Kannada stage.
He died in 1891, honoured as the father of Kannada theatre. His plays and his vision founded the stage of the language, and his name remains the greatest in the early history of Kannada drama.

items.name: Mudaveedu Krishnarao
items.tagline: The lion of the Kannada stage — the master of the heroic role
items.attribution: Mudaveedu Krishnarao — the actor of the Kannada stage
items.quote: Play the hero so that the people leave the theatre taller — the stage builds the nation.
items.summary: Mudaveedu Krishnarao was one of the great actors of the Kannada stage — a performer of heroic roles whose acting moved audiences to their feet and whose patriotic plays stirred the spirit of the people. He was also a man of deep pride in his land, language, and faith, and his life was a service to the culture of Karnataka.
overview: Born in 1899, Mudaveedu Krishnarao was drawn to the theatre in his youth and rose to become one of the leading actors of the Kannada stage. He was famous for the heroic roles — the kings and warriors of the historical and mythological plays — and his performances, full of power and dignity, made him a beloved figure of the people.

The account of his life records that his speeches and his plays moved audiences to a thrill of patriotism — he was a master of the patriotic drama who used the stage to awaken the pride of the people in their land and their culture. His pride in his religion, language, and country was deep, but it never became arrogance.

He died in 1983, honoured as the lion of the Kannada stage. His performances are remembered as among the greatest of the modern theatre of Karnataka, and his life was a service to the culture of his people.

items.name: Mysore Sadashivarao
items.tagline: The singer-composer of Mysore — the voice of Kannada music
items.attribution: Mysore Sadashivarao — the singer and composer
items.quote: The song of the land must be sung by the voice of the land — compose for the people.
items.summary: Mysore Sadashivarao was one of the great figures of the music of Karnataka — a singer of a sweet voice and a composer of beautiful songs whose work enriched the Carnatic tradition of the South. He was also a teacher who guided a generation of musicians, and his life was one of purity and service to the art.
overview: Born in 1890 in Mysore, Sadashivarao grew up in the richest musical atmosphere of the South — the court of the Wodeyar maharajas — and his voice was recognised as a gift of rare beauty. He trained in the Carnatic tradition and became one of the leading singers of the region.

He was also a composer of distinction: he wrote songs of great sweetness, and his compositions — both in the classical style and in the lighter forms of the land — were loved by the people. He guided a number of great musicians under his tutelage, and his life, as his biographers record, was pure and clean.

He died in 1975, honoured as one of the great musicians of Mysore. His songs and his teaching enriched the music of the South, and his name is remembered with respect in the musical tradition of Karnataka.

items.name: Papanasam Sivan
items.tagline: The Tamil Tyagaraja — the composer of the devotional song
items.attribution: Papanasam Sivan — the composer and singer
items.quote: The song is the prayer of the South — let it be sung in the language of the people.
items.summary: Papanasam Sivan was one of the greatest composers of Carnatic music — the 'Tamil Tyagaraja', whose devotional kritis in Tamil are sung in every concert of the South. His songs, born of his devotion and his love of the Tamil language, made him one of the most beloved figures of the Carnatic tradition.
overview: Born in 1890 in Papanasam, Sivan was trained in music and Sanskrit and became a master of the Carnatic tradition. His devotion was the soul of his art: he was a worshipper of the Lord and a singer whose songs were prayers, and his fame as a composer grew across the Tamil land.

He composed more than a thousand kritis, mostly in Tamil, in which he carried the depth of the Carnatic tradition into the language of the people. His songs — including the beloved compositions of the classical ragas — are sung in every concert of the South, and he is honoured as the Tamil Tyagaraja.

He also acted in the early Tamil cinema, singing his own compositions on the screen, and died in 1973, honoured as one of the greatest composers of the tradition. His songs remain the treasure of the South, and his name is remembered with devotion.

items.name: Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar
items.tagline: The architect of the modern Carnatic concert
items.attribution: Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar — the Carnatic vocalist
items.quote: The concert is a temple of the raga — let every item build toward the silence of the soul.
items.summary: Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar was one of the greatest Carnatic vocalists of the modern age — the musician who designed the format of the modern Carnatic concert, arranging its items in the order that every concert follows today. His singing, marked by its clarity and its sweetness, made him the model of the Carnatic vocalist for a century.
overview: Born in 1890 in Ariyakudi, Ramanuja Iyengar was trained in music from childhood and became a master of the Carnatic vocal art. He developed the structure of the concert — the format of opening varnam, kritis, and the concluding pieces — that became the standard of every Carnatic concert, and which is followed to this day.

His singing was the model of the tradition: his voice was sweet and clear, his diction perfect, and his rendering of the kritis — especially the compositions of Tyagaraja — was the standard of the age. He was honoured with the title of Sangeetha Kalanidhi and honoured across the South.

He died in 1967, honoured as the architect of the modern Carnatic concert. His format, his style, and his singing shaped the music of the South for a century, and his name remains one of the greatest in the Carnatic tradition.

items.name: A.V. Varadachariar
items.tagline: The actor of the Kannada and Tamil stage — the reformer of the theatre
items.attribution: A.V. Varadachariar — the actor of the stage
items.quote: The stage must grow with the age — reform the theatre, and you reform the people.
items.summary: A.V. Varadachariar was a great actor of the Kannada stage who won an immortal place in the history of the theatre of the region — a performer whose art captivated audiences in Karnataka and in the Tamil country alike. He was also a reformer of the stage and a man of generous character.
overview: Born in 1898, Varadachariar was drawn to the theatre and became one of the leading actors of the Kannada stage. His acting won him an immortal place in the history of the theatre of the land — the account of his life in the Bharata Bharati series records that his performances were among the glories of the stage.

He reformed the theatre in many ways, raising its standards and its art, and his fame spread beyond Karnataka — he captivated the people of the Tamil country as well, where his performances were equally adored. He was also known as a senior artist of generous character, a free-handed donor.
He died in 1976, honoured as one of the great actors of the stage of the South. His art and his reforms are part of the golden history of the Kannada and Tamil theatre.

items.name: Prithviraj Kapoor
items.tagline: The patriarch of the Kapoor dynasty — the titan of Indian cinema and stage
items.attribution: Prithviraj Kapoor — actor of stage and screen
items.quote: The theatre is the temple of the people — and the actor is its priest.
items.summary: Prithviraj Kapoor was one of the greatest actors of Indian cinema and the father of the most famous acting dynasty of Bhārat — the patriarch of the Kapoors who dominated the screen for three generations. He was also the founder of Prithvi Theatres, the great travelling stage company, and his voice and presence made him a titan of the Indian stage and screen.
overview: Born in 1906 in Lyallpur, Prithviraj Kapoor was drawn to acting against the wishes of his family and made his way to Bombay, where he entered the world of the silent and early talkie cinema. His powerful voice and his majestic presence made him one of the leading actors of the 1930s and 1940s.

He was equally great on the stage: he founded Prithvi Theatres in 1944, a travelling company that took classic Hindi plays to the towns of Bhārat, and the company's productions became the most famous in the land. His sons Raj, Shammi, and Shashi — and his grandsons — carried his name to the heights of the cinema.

His greatest film role was that of Emperor Akbar in Mughal-e-Azam, the epic that remains a classic of world cinema. He died in 1972, honoured as the patriarch of the greatest acting family of Bhārat and one of the titans of its stage and screen.

items.name: Balraj Sahni
items.tagline: The actor of truth — the beloved star of Indian cinema
items.attribution: Balraj Sahni — the actor
items.quote: Act with the truth of the heart — the camera can see a lie a mile away.
items.summary: Balraj Sahni was one of the most loved actors of Indian cinema — a star whose natural, truthful acting made him the model of the realist performer. His role in the classic Do Bigha Zamin made him a national icon, and his life, marked by integrity and simplicity, made him as loved as a man as he was as an artist.
overview: Born in 1913 in Rawalpindi, Balraj Sahni was an educated man — he studied at Lahore and London — who entered the cinema in the 1940s. He brought to the screen a naturalness and a truth that were new to Indian acting, and he rose to become one of its most beloved stars.

His greatest role came in 1953 in Do Bigha Zamin, the classic story of a poor farmer — a film whose realism and humanity made him a national icon and established the new wave of Indian cinema. He acted in more than sixty films, always with the same truth and simplicity, and he also wrote with skill.

He died in 1973, and the nation mourned one of its most loved actors. He is remembered not only for his art but for his life — a man of integrity who was as respected for his simplicity as he was loved for his acting.

items.name: Guru Dutt
items.tagline: The poet of the cinema — the genius of the tragic frame
items.attribution: Guru Dutt — the filmmaker and actor
items.quote: The cinema is poetry — and the frame is the line of the poem.
items.summary: Guru Dutt was one of the greatest filmmakers of the world — the poet of Indian cinema whose films, especially Pyaasa and Kaagaz Ke Phool, are counted among the masterpieces of world cinema. An actor and director of genius, he died young, but his films — dark, lyrical, and heartbreakingly beautiful — made him immortal.
overview: Born in 1925 in Bangalore, Guru Dutt entered the cinema in the 1940s, first as a dancer and then as an actor and director. His first great success as a director, Baazi, launched him in 1951, and he became one of the most original talents of the Indian screen.

His masterpieces — Pyaasa (1957), the story of a neglected poet, and Kaagaz Ke Phool (1959), the tragedy of a filmmaker — are among the most beautiful and most melancholy films ever made. His use of light, shadow, and song, and his vision of the artist crushed by the world, made him the poet of the cinema.

He died in 1964, at just thirty-nine, in the sadness that pervaded his art. His films, long underrated, are now honoured as masterpieces of world cinema, and his name is spoken with the greatest directors of the world.

items.name: M.G. Ramachandran
items.tagline: The matinee idol of the South — the star who became a Chief Minister
items.attribution: M.G. Ramachandran — the actor and Chief Minister
items.region: Kandy, Sri Lanka; raised in Tamil Nadu
items.quote: The star belongs to the people — and the people's welfare is the star's true role.
items.summary: M.G. Ramachandran, known to millions as MGR, was the greatest star of Tamil cinema — the hero of more than a hundred films whose screen roles made him the idol of the poor of the South. He carried that love into politics, founded his own party, and became the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, serving the people he had entertained for three decades.
overview: Born in 1917 in Kandy and raised in poverty, MGR entered the theatre and then the cinema, where his roles as the hero who fights for the poor made him the most beloved star of the South. From the 1950s he dominated the Tamil screen, his films — full of action, charity, and justice — making him the idol of millions.

He entered politics through the DMK and then founded his own party, the AIADMK, in 1972. In 1977 he became the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, and he governed for nearly a decade, loved by the people as few leaders have been — his welfare schemes and his simple life making him a legend.

He died in 1987, and his funeral was one of the largest in the history of the world. He is remembered as the matinee idol who became a Chief Minister — a star whose life, on screen and off, was devoted to the poor he had made his audience and his people.

items.name: N.T. Rama Rao
items.tagline: NTR — the mythological hero of the screen who ruled Andhra
items.attribution: N.T. Rama Rao — the actor and Chief Minister
items.quote: Play the god on the screen and you owe the people a god's devotion in life.
items.quoteSource: The spirit of N.T. Rama Rao
items.summary: N.T. Rama Rao, known as NTR, was the greatest star of Telugu cinema — the actor who played the gods of the epics, especially Krishna, with such power that millions worshipped him on the screen. He carried that devotion into politics, founded the Telugu Desam Party in a single week, and became the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh.
overview: Born in 1923 in Nimmakuru, NTR entered the cinema in 1949 and rose to become the greatest star of the Telugu screen. His roles as Krishna, Rama, and the heroes of the epics — especially his Krishna in the classic films — made him a living god to millions, and his films were among the most beloved of the South.

In 1982, at the height of his fame, he founded the Telugu Desam Party — a party built in a single week on his name — and in 1983 he became the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, the first film star to rule a state as the head of his own party. He served as Chief Minister twice, loved by the masses.

He died in 1996, and his passing was mourned by millions. He is remembered as the mythological hero of the screen who ruled Andhra — an actor whose god-like roles made him the idol and then the leader of a whole people.

items.name: S.S. Vasan
items.tagline: The pioneer of Tamil cinema — the maker of the epic screen
items.attribution: S.S. Vasan — the filmmaker and publisher
items.quote: The cinema of the people must be made with the scale of the epic — give them the grandeur they dream of.
items.summary: S.S. Vasan was one of the great pioneers of Indian cinema — the filmmaker and publisher who made the epic scale of Tamil cinema possible. His Gemini Studios produced some of the greatest films of the age, including the immortal Chandralekha, and his magazine, Ananda Vikatan, was the most influential of the Tamil world.
overview: Born in 1903, Vasan was a journalist who took over the Ananda Vikatan, the great Tamil magazine, and made it the most influential publication of the language. He then entered the cinema, founding Gemini Studios, which became one of the greatest film studios of India.

His Chandralekha (1948) was the first great epic of Indian cinema — a film of astonishing scale whose drum-beat finale became world-famous. Under his hand Gemini Studios produced a series of the greatest films of the age, and his vision of the grand, popular cinema shaped the Tamil screen.

He died in 1969, honoured as one of the founders of the Indian film industry. His studio, his films, and his magazine made him one of the most powerful and influential figures of the culture of the South.

items.name: Gubbi Veeranna
items.tagline: The king of the Kannada stage — the maker of the people's theatre
items.attribution: Gubbi Veeranna — the theatre pioneer of Karnataka
items.quote: The theatre belongs to the people — take it to every town and every village of the land.
items.summary: Gubbi Veeranna was the king of the Kannada stage — the theatre pioneer who built the most famous drama company of Karnataka and carried the stage to every town of the state. His Gubbi company trained a generation of actors and produced the plays that are the golden history of Kannada theatre.
overview: Born in 1891 in Gubbi, Veeranna founded his drama company in his youth and built it into the greatest theatrical organisation of Karnataka. His company toured the towns and villages of the state, staging the mythological, historical, and social plays of the age with a professionalism that set the standard of the Kannada stage.

He was not only a producer but a mentor: his company trained some of the finest actors and actresses of the Kannada stage and screen, and his productions — with their music, their spectacle, and their craft — made the theatre the entertainment of the people for half a century.

He was honoured with the Padma Bhushan and the title of the king of the Kannada stage. He died in 1972, and his name remains the greatest in the history of the theatre of Karnataka — the man who took the stage to the people.

items.name: Mario Miranda
items.tagline: The cartoonist of genius — who drew the laughter of the world
items.attribution: Mario Miranda — the cartoonist
items.quote: The cartoonist is the mirror of the street — draw what you see, and let the world laugh at itself.
items.summary: Mario Miranda was one of the greatest cartoonists of the world — the artist of Goa whose witty, detailed drawings of the life of the street made him the most beloved cartoonist of Bhārat. His work appeared in the world's greatest newspapers and magazines, and his art was honoured with the Padma Vibhushan and with exhibitions across the globe.
overview: Born in 1926 in Loutolim, Goa, Mario Miranda studied art in Bombay and began his career as a cartoonist with the Times of India, where his daily cartoons made him famous across the country. His style — detailed, comic, and full of the life of the street — was instantly recognisable and universally loved.

His work appeared in publications across the world, from the newspapers of Bhārat to the great magazines of Europe, and his drawings of the people, the markets, and the everyday scenes of the land became a treasured record of its life. He drew with affection, and the world laughed with him, not at his subjects.

He was honoured with the Padma Shri and the Padma Vibhushan and with exhibitions in the great cities of the world. He died in 2011, and his name remains the greatest in the cartoon art of Bhārat — the artist who drew the laughter of the world.

items.name: K.K. Hebbar
items.tagline: The master of the modern canvas — the painter of the Indian soul
items.attribution: Kattingeri Krishna Hebbar — the painter
items.quote: The modern brush must carry the soul of the land — paint the music, the dance, and the people.
items.summary: K.K. Hebbar was one of the greatest painters of modern Bhārat — the artist of the coast whose canvases, full of the music, the dance, and the life of the land, carried the soul of Bhārat into the modern idiom. His work is honoured in the great museums and collections of the world, and he was one of the founders of the modern art movement of the nation.
overview: Born in 1911 in Kattingeri near Udupi, Hebbar studied art in Bombay and, in the 1940s, became one of the leading figures of the modern art movement of Bhārat. His early work — paintings of the famine and the suffering of the people — was powerful, and his style grew into a masterful synthesis of the modern and the Indian.

His greatest canvases are those of the music and dance of the land — his paintings of the tabla player, the veena, and the dancers of Bhārat are among the most famous works of modern Indian art. He painted the people and the life of his coast with a colour and a rhythm that are unmistakably his own.

He was honoured with the Padma Bhushan and with exhibitions across the world, and his works are in the great collections of Bhārat and abroad. He died in 1996, honoured as one of the founders of modern Indian painting.

items.name: C. Aswath
items.tagline: The master of Bhavageethe — the voice that set Kannada poetry to song
items.attribution: C. Aswath — the singer and composer
items.quote: The poem must be sung as the poet dreamed it — the song is the poem's true life.
items.summary: C. Aswath was the master of Bhavageethe — the art of setting Kannada poetry to music — and one of the most loved musicians of Karnataka. For four decades his voice carried the poems of the great Kannada poets into the homes of the people, and his music became the very sound of the modern Kannada cultural awakening.
overview: Born in 1939, Aswath was trained in music and drawn to the songs of the poets. He developed the art of Bhavageethe — the musical setting of the great Kannada poems — and his concerts, beginning in the 1970s, made him one of the most popular musicians of the state.

His voice and his arrangements brought the poems of Kuvempu, Bendre, and the other great poets of the language to the people in a way that made them live again. His songs — from the soaring to the tender — became the soundtrack of the Kannada cultural awakening, and his concerts drew audiences that filled the halls.
He died in 2009, and the whole of Karnataka mourned the voice that had sung its poetry for four decades. He is honoured as the master of Bhavageethe — the musician who gave the Kannada poem its song.

items.name: Mysore Ananthaswamy
items.tagline: The pioneer of Sugama Sangeetha — the voice of Kannada light music
items.attribution: Mysore Ananthaswamy — the singer and composer
items.quote: The light song must not be light in art — let the simple song carry the deepest feeling.
items.summary: Mysore Ananthaswamy was the pioneer of Sugama Sangeetha, the light music of Karnataka — a singer and composer who set the poems of the great Kannada poets to music and created a whole genre of the state's music. His songs, simple and beautiful, are among the most loved in the Kannada language.
overview: Born in 1936 in Mysore, Ananthaswamy was trained in music and began his career as a composer in the 1960s. He created the style of Sugama Sangeetha — the 'easy music' that set the poems of Kuvempu, Bendre, and other great poets to melodies of rare simplicity and beauty.

His songs, sung by the people of Karnataka for decades, made him one of the most loved musicians of the state. He composed for the stage, the radio, and the films of the land, and his music carried the Kannada poem to the common listener in a way no one had done before.

He died in 1995, honoured as the pioneer of Sugama Sangeetha. His songs remain the treasure of the state's music, and his name is remembered as the founder of the genre that made the Kannada poem sing.

items.name: S.G. Bindu Rao
items.tagline: The master of Gamaka — the singer of the Kumaravyasa Bharata
items.attribution: S.G. Bindu Rao — the Gamaka artist
items.quote: The Gamaka is the song of the epic — recite the Bharata so that the heart of the listener trembles.
items.quoteSource: The spirit of S.G. Bindu Rao
items.summary: S.G. Bindu Rao was one of the greatest masters of Gamaka — the art of singing the classics of Kannada with musical interpretation — and his recitation of the Kumaravyasa Bharata was famous across the land. He was the artist who kept the ancient art of the Gamaka alive and trained a generation in its mastery.
overview: Born in 1893, Bindu Rao mastered the art of the Gamaka — the musical recitation of the great Kannada classics, in which the singer interprets the poetry with melody and rhythm. His art was the inheritance of the Karnataka tradition, and he became one of its greatest exponents.

His recitation of the Kumaravyasa Bharata, the great Kannada Mahabharata, was the wonder of the age — he sang the epic so sweetly and so movingly that the whole of the Kannada land came to hear him. His performances kept the ancient art alive at a time when it was fading, and he trained many disciples to carry it forward.
He died in 1970, honoured as one of the greatest Gamaka artists of the age. His art is remembered as the living voice of the Kannada epic, and his name is honoured wherever the Gamaka is sung.

items.name: Keremane Shivaram Hegde
items.tagline: The king of Yakshagana — the master of the great coastal art
items.attribution: Keremane Shivaram Hegde — the Yakshagana artist
items.quote: The Yakshagana is the epic made visible — the dance, the drum, and the god on the open stage.
items.quoteSource: The spirit of Keremane Shivaram Hegde
items.summary: Keremane Shivaram Hegde was the king of Yakshagana — the great dance-drama of the Karnataka coast — and one of the most celebrated artists in its history. As the leader of the famous Yakshagana troupe of his village, he carried the art to the stages of Bhārat and the world, and his performances made him a legend of the coastal land.
overview: Born in 1908 in Keremane, on the coast of Karnataka, Shivaram Hegde grew up in the world of the Yakshagana — the great open-air dance-drama of the region, in which the epics are enacted with drums, dance, and magnificent costumes. He became its master, both as a performer of the great roles and as a leader of the art.

He founded the famous Yakshagana troupe of Keremane, which became the most celebrated company of the art, and he carried the Yakshagana from the village stages of the coast to the festivals and stages of the nation and the world. His performances of the great roles were the wonder of the audiences.
He was honoured with the Padma Shri and the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award. He died in 1991, and his name remains the greatest in the modern history of the Yakshagana — the king of the art of the coast.

items.name: Maha Vaidyanatha Iyer
items.tagline: The prodigy of Carnatic music — the composer of the Ragamalika
items.attribution: Maha Vaidyanatha Iyer — the singer and composer
items.quote: Sing so that even the great scholars bow their heads — and compose for the glory of the Lord.
items.quoteSource: The spirit of Maha Vaidyanatha Iyer
items.summary: Maha Vaidyanatha Iyer was a prodigy of Carnatic music — a singer who, from the age of ten, astonished the great scholars of the South, and a composer whose work includes one of the greatest creations of the tradition, the Ragamalika of 108 ragas. His genius and his humility made him one of the most revered musicians of his age.
overview: Born in 1844 in Thanjavur, Vaidyanatha Iyer was a prodigy whose voice and talent amazed all who heard him — the account of his life records that from the age of ten he sang in a manner that made the most learned scholars nod in admiration. He was trained in the tradition of the great composers of the South.

His greatest creation is the monumental Ragamalika — a composition that passes through 108 ragas, the supreme display of the Carnatic art, sung to this day as the wonder of the tradition. He also composed many other works, always with the same mastery and the same devotion.

He died in 1893, honoured as one of the greatest musicians of the age. His genius was matched by his humility — he dedicated all his music to the Lord and lived a life of detachment, and his name remains among the greatest of the Carnatic tradition.

items.name: M. Venkatakrishnayya
items.tagline: The teacher-journalist of the Kannada land — the society's conscience
items.attribution: M. Venkatakrishnayya — teacher and journalist
items.quote: The teacher and the journalist are the conscience of the society — keep the truth clean.
items.summary: M. Venkatakrishnayya was a teacher and journalist of the Kannada land — a man born in poverty who never knew wealth but whose heart and life were rich beyond measure. He was among the foremost of the pioneers of Kannada journalism, a teacher of ideals, and a voice of the society's conscience for half a century.
overview: Born in 1878 in poverty, Venkatakrishnayya rose by his own efforts to become a teacher — an ideal teacher, as the account of his life records — and then a journalist. He was among the earliest and most senior pioneers of Kannada journalism, and his work in the press shaped the public life of the state.

He never knew the wealth of money, but his heart and his life were rich: he was called the grandfather, the ocean of compassion, the Bhishmacharya of the Kannada press by the society that honoured him. He worked for the language, the nation, and the truth all his life.

He died in 1955, honoured as the society's conscience. His life — the poor teacher and journalist who became the father figure of his profession — remains a model of integrity and service to the Kannada land.

items.name: Veene Venkatagiriyappa
items.tagline: The master of the veena — the heir of the great Sheshanna
items.attribution: Venkatagiriyappa — the veena player
items.quote: The veena speaks the raga — and the raga speaks the soul of the tradition.
items.summary: Veene Venkatagiriyappa was one of the great masters of the veena — the disciple of the legendary Veene Sheshanna who also mastered the Western music of the age. A simple and generous man, he gave music lessons to hundreds of students and his playing was among the glories of the Mysore tradition.
overview: Born in 1886, Venkatagiriyappa was trained in the veena by the greatest master of the instrument, Veene Sheshanna, and he became one of the finest players of the age. He was a musician of remarkable range — he also mastered the Western music of the time, a rare accomplishment for the musicians of the South.

He was a teacher of generosity: he gave music lessons to hundreds of students, and his simple, liberal nature made him beloved. He appreciated the worth of others without jealousy, and his playing of the veena was counted among the glories of the Mysore tradition.
He died in 1948, honoured as one of the great masters of the veena. His students carried his tradition across the land, and his name is remembered with respect in the musical history of Karnataka.

items.name: Shyama Shastri
items.tagline: One of the Trinity of Carnatic music — the singer of the goddess
items.attribution: Shyama Shastri — the composer of the Carnatic Trinity
items.quote: The goddess is my mother — and the song is the child's speech to the mother.
items.summary: Shyama Shastri was one of the Trinity of Carnatic music — the trio of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, and Shyama Shastri who created the golden age of the South's music. He was the eldest of the three, and his compositions, full of devotion to the goddess and of musical genius, are among the treasures of the Carnatic tradition.
overview: Born in 1762 in Thanjavur, Shyama Shastri was trained in music and became a devotee of the goddess Kamakshi of Thanjavur. His compositions were born of his devotion — the songs of the goddess that he poured out are among the most beautiful in the Carnatic tradition.

He was one of the Trinity of Carnatic music — with Tyagaraja and Muthuswami Dikshitar — who together created the golden age of the art. His compositions, marked by their depth and their subtle mastery of the ragas, are sung in every concert of the South.

He died in 1827, honoured as one of the greatest composers of the tradition. His songs of the goddess remain the treasure of the Carnatic music, and his name stands with the Trinity at the summit of the art.

items.name: Mahadev Govind Ranade
items.tagline: The father of the Indian renaissance — the judge who reformed the nation
items.attribution: Mahadev Govind Ranade — judge, scholar, and reformer
items.quote: Reform society, and the nation will reform itself — the home is the seed of the state.
items.summary: Mahadev Govind Ranade was the father of the Indian renaissance — a judge of the Bombay High Court, a scholar, and the greatest social reformer of the age. He founded the Prarthana Samaj, championed the rights of women, and argued that the progress of the nation must begin with the reform of its society.
overview: Born in 1842 in Niphad, Ranade was a brilliant student who rose to become a judge of the Bombay High Court — one of the first Indians to reach such a position. But his real mission was the reform of society: he founded the Prarthana Samaj, the prayer society that worked for a purified and rational religion, and the Deccan Education movement's institutions of learning.

He was the champion of women's rights in an age of orthodoxy: he opposed child marriage, supported widow remarriage, and worked for the education of women. His great work, The Rise of the Maratha Power, and his essays made him the leading intellectual of the reform movement.

He died in 1901, and the whole nation honoured him as the father of the modern renaissance. Gandhi himself acknowledged his debt to Ranade's thought, and his vision — that social reform must accompany political freedom — became the foundation of the modern Indian awakening.

His ideas influenced Gandhi and every reformer after him, and his name remains the foundation of the social reform movement of Bhārat.

items.name: Siddavanahalli Krishna Sharma
items.tagline: The freedom fighter and journalist of the Hyderabad struggle
items.attribution: Siddavanahalli Krishna Sharma — freedom fighter and journalist
items.quote: The pen must serve the awakening of the people — write so that the nation may stand tall.
items.summary: Siddavanahalli Krishna Sharma was a freedom fighter, journalist, and writer who played a heroic role in the awakening of the Hyderabad state — the man who worked to stir the people against the oppressive rule of the Nizam. A brilliant orator and one of the architects of modern Kannada prose, he gave his life to the service of the nation.
overview: Born in 1887 in Siddavanahalli, Krishna Sharma was drawn to the national movement in his youth. He worked for the awakening of the Hyderabad state, where the people suffered under the autocratic rule of the Nizam, and his writings and his courage made him a leading figure of the struggle.

He was a journalist who used the press to serve the people, and a writer who helped shape modern Kannada prose — the account of his life records that he was one of the great architects of the language's modern prose style. He was also an extraordinary orator whose speeches stirred the people.
He died in 1954, honoured as a hero of the freedom struggle of the Hyderabad region. His life — the pen, the platform, and the prison — remains a model of the complete patriot.

items.name: Gopal Krishna Devadhar
items.tagline: The disciple of Gokhale — the servant of the nation's poor
items.attribution: Gopal Krishna Devadhar — the worker of the Servants of India Society
items.quote: The service of the people is the worship of the nation — and the poor are its temple.
items.summary: Gopal Krishna Devadhar was one of the greatest workers of the Servants of India Society — the disciple of Gopal Krishna Gokhale who devoted his life to the service of the poor and the reform of society. He worked in the famine relief of the land, in the uplift of the depressed classes, and in every cause of the nation's welfare.
overview: Born in 1871, Devadhar was drawn to the ideals of Gokhale, the great leader who believed that the service of the people was the true politics of the nation. He joined the Servants of India Society and devoted his life to its work — the service of the poor and the reform of society.

His work ranged across the nation's needs: he served in the great famine relief operations, worked for the uplift of the depressed classes, and served in education and rural welfare. He was a man of tireless energy who held no office for himself but gave everything to the people.

He died in 1934, honoured as one of the greatest servants of the nation's poor. His life — the complete gift of a brilliant man to the service of others — remains the model of the Servants of India Society's ideal.

items.name: Sane Guruji
items.tagline: The teacher who loved all — the Gandhi of the children of Maharashtra
items.attribution: Pandurang Sadashiv Sane — 'Sane Guruji'
items.quote: Let me be the friend of every child, the servant of every poor person, and the lover of the whole world.
items.summary: Sane Guruji was one of the most loved teachers and writers of Maharashtra — a Gandhian whose love for children, the poor, and the whole of humanity made him a legend. His Shyamchi Aai, the story of a mother's love, is among the most beloved books of the Marathi language, and his life of service made him the Gandhi of the children of the land.
overview: Born in 1899 in Palgad, Pandurang Sadashiv Sane — Sane Guruji — was a teacher whose love for his students knew no bounds. He joined the freedom movement under Gandhi's leadership and devoted his life to the service of the nation, teaching, writing, and working among the poor.

His great book, Shyamchi Aai — 'Shyam's mother' — told the story of his own childhood and the love of his mother, and it became one of the most beloved books of the Marathi language, read in every home. He wrote dozens of books for children and the people, full of love and idealism.

He died in 1950, at just fifty-one, worn out by his labours and his sorrow at the nation's divisions. He is honoured as the Gandhi of the children of Maharashtra — a teacher whose love for all beings made him one of the most beloved figures of the land.

items.name: Thakkar Bapa
items.tagline: The father of the tribal people — Gandhi's servant of the adivasis
items.attribution: Amritlal Vithaldas Thakkar — 'Thakkar Bapa'
items.quote: The adivasi is my brother — and the hills and forests of the land are my home.
items.summary: Thakkar Bapa was the father of the tribal people of Bhārat — the servant of Gandhi who devoted his life to the uplift of the adivasis, the tribal peoples of the hills and forests. For fifty years he lived among them, served them, and fought for their rights, and he is honoured as the greatest friend the tribal people of the land have had.
overview: Born in 1869 in Bhavnagar, Amritlal Thakkar was an engineer who left his career to serve the people. He came under Gandhi's influence and devoted his life to the cause of the adivasis — the tribal peoples whom the nation had forgotten — and he was given the name Thakkar Bapa, the father, by the people he served.

He worked among the tribal communities of Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Central India for half a century, living their life, learning their languages, and serving their needs — in health, education, and land rights. He founded the Bharatiya Adimjati Sevak Sangh, the society for the service of the tribal peoples, and his work made him their greatest champion.

He died in 1951, honoured as the father of the tribal people. His life — the complete gift of a servant to the forgotten of the land — remains the model of service, and his name is remembered with love wherever the adivasis live.

His name is remembered with love wherever the tribal people live, and his life remains the model of service to the forgotten of the land.

items.name: P. Kodanda Rao
items.tagline: The servant of the nation — the worker of the Servants of India Society
items.attribution: P. Kodanda Rao — the worker of the Servants of India Society
items.quote: Serve the people of the nation wherever they are — the service knows no boundary of caste or land.
items.summary: P. Kodanda Rao was a devoted worker of the Servants of India Society — the organisation of Gopal Krishna Gokhale — who served the people of Bhārat for a lifetime. He worked both in Bhārat and abroad for the welfare of the nation's people, and he was known for the fearlessness and balance of his opinions.
overview: Born in 1889, Kodanda Rao decided, even as his student days were ending, to dedicate his life to the service of the country. He joined the Servants of India Society, the great organisation of Gokhale, and devoted himself wholly to its work.

He served the people of Bhārat without regard to distinctions of caste or community, working both in the land and abroad — in the countries where the people of Bhārat had gone — for their welfare. He was known for the fearlessness and balance of his opinions, and his voice was heard with respect in public life.
He died in 1980, honoured as one of the devoted servants of the nation. His life — the complete gift of a man to the service of the people — remains a model of the Servants of India Society's ideal.

items.name: Muthulakshmi Reddy
items.tagline: The first woman doctor of Madras — the champion of women's rights
items.attribution: Muthulakshmi Reddy — the physician and reformer
items.quote: The health and dignity of the woman is the foundation of the nation — serve both.
items.summary: Muthulakshmi Reddy was a pioneer of modern Bhārat — one of the first women doctors of the land, a legislator, and a lifelong champion of women's rights. She fought against the evil of the devadasi system, worked for the education and health of women, and founded the Avvai Home for the care of the abandoned.
overview: Born in 1886 in Madras, Muthulakshmi Reddy broke every barrier of her age: she became one of the first women doctors of the land, and then one of the first women legislators of the Madras legislature. Her life was devoted to the uplift of women, whom the age had left behind.

She led the campaign against the devadasi system, the custom that condemned young women to a life of exploitation, and she worked to give the victims of the system education and a place in society. She founded the Avvai Home for the care of orphaned and abandoned girls and worked for their welfare all her life.

She died in 1968, honoured as one of the great women of modern Bhārat. Her life — the doctor, the legislator, and the champion of women — remains a model of the reformer, and her name is honoured wherever the rights of women are cherished.

items.name: Viresalingam Pantulu
items.tagline: The father of the Andhra renaissance — the reformer of the Telugu land
items.attribution: Kandukuri Viresalingam — the reformer and writer of Andhra
items.quote: The widow's tears and the child bride's sorrow — these are the stains the reformer must wash away.
items.summary: Viresalingam Pantulu was the father of the Andhra renaissance — the reformer, writer, and educator who transformed the society of the Telugu land. He fought against child marriage and the misery of widows, championed widow remarriage, and created the modern prose and literature of Telugu, becoming one of the greatest reformers of the age.
overview: Born in 1848 in Rajahmundry, Viresalingam was a scholar of Telugu and Sanskrit who devoted his life to the reform of his society. He attacked the evils of child marriage and the terrible condition of widows, and he championed the cause of widow remarriage with a courage that defied the orthodoxy of his age.

He was also the creator of the modern Telugu language and literature: he wrote the first Telugu novels, the first autobiography, and countless essays and works that shaped modern Telugu prose. He founded schools and journals, and his home became the centre of the Andhra renaissance.

He died in 1919, honoured as the father of the Andhra renaissance. His reforms and his writings transformed the Telugu land, and his name remains the greatest in the modern history of the language and society of Andhra.

items.name: Ammembal Subba Rao Pai
items.tagline: The benefactor of the coast — the founder of the Canara Bank
items.attribution: Ammembal Subba Rao Pai — banker and philanthropist
items.quote: Educate the people and the nation rises — the bank of the people must serve the people's future.
items.summary: Ammembal Subba Rao Pai was one of the greatest benefactors of the Karnataka coast — the founder of the Canara Bank, which grew into one of the great banks of the nation, and a philanthropist who gave his wealth to education and the welfare of the people. His life was a model of the union of enterprise and generosity.
overview: Born in 1852 in Mangaluru, Subba Rao Pai was a lawyer who, in 1906, founded the Canara Hindu Permanent Fund — the institution that grew into the Canara Bank, one of the great banks of the nation. His vision was a bank of the people, rooted in the coastal land, that would serve their needs and their future.

His generosity was extraordinary: he gave lakhs for education, founding schools and colleges, and his philanthropy transformed the opportunities of the young people of the coast. He was also a supporter of the national movement and of the cause of the people.

He died in 1909, at just fifty-seven. His bank grew into a national institution, and his gifts to education continue to serve the land. He is honoured as one of the greatest sons of the Karnataka coast.

items.name: Manjaya Heggade
items.tagline: The Dharmadhikari of Dharmasthala — the servant of the temple's charity
items.attribution: Manjaya Heggade — the Dharmadhikari of Dharmasthala
items.quote: The temple's wealth is the people's trust — feed the hungry, and the Lord is pleased.
items.summary: Manjaya Heggade was the Dharmadhikari — the administrator of charity — of the great temple of Dharmasthala, one of the most sacred and charitable institutions of the South. Under his stewardship the temple's vast charity served the poor, the sick, and the students of the land, and his name is honoured as the model of the servant of the people's trust.
overview: Dharmasthala, the great temple of the South, has been served for centuries by the Heggade family, whose title Dharmadhikari means 'the administrator of charity'. Manjaya Heggade, born in 1888, carried that trust in the twentieth century, guiding the temple's vast works of charity and service.

Under his stewardship the temple's charity reached every need of the people — the feeding of the hungry, the care of the sick, the education of the young, and the help of the poor. He held the trust as a sacred duty, and his life was a service to the people of the land.

He died in 1968, honoured as one of the great servants of the temple's charity. His name is remembered with reverence at Dharmasthala, and his stewardship remains the model of the Dharmadhikari's trust.

items.name: Kudmul Ranga Rao
items.tagline: The crusader against untouchability — the reformer of the coast
items.attribution: Kudmul Ranga Rao — the social reformer
items.quote: The barriers of caste are the chains of the nation — break them, and the nation is free.
items.summary: Kudmul Ranga Rao was a pioneer social reformer of the Karnataka coast — one of the first crusaders against untouchability in the region. A generation before Gandhi made the cause national, he worked for the uplift of the depressed classes, for their education, and for the end of the caste barriers that divided the land.
overview: Born in 1854 in Mangaluru, Ranga Rao was a lawyer and a man of the Bunt community who was deeply troubled by the evil of untouchability. In an age when the subject was rarely spoken of, he began to work for the uplift of the depressed classes of the coast, becoming one of the first reformers of the region to take up the cause.

He worked for the education of the depressed classes, founded schools for them, and campaigned against the barriers of caste that excluded them from the common life. His work anticipated by decades the national movement against untouchability, and he carried it forward with courage in the face of orthodoxy.

He died in 1932, honoured as a pioneer of the reform movement of the coast. His name is remembered as one of the first champions of the cause of equality in the region, and his work laid the foundation for the reforms that followed.
